title: United States: White House hard-pass deactivations for CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters, September 2026
outcome_note: Cable News Network, Inc. v. Trump (D.D.C. No. 1:26-cv-03287) was filed on 2026-09-21 and is pending; a hearing is scheduled for 2026-09-23.
summary: On September 18, 2026, the president of the United States, Donald Trump, announced on Truth Social, a social media platform, and in the Oval Office that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be banned from the White House, the president's office and residence in Washington, D.C. He described the outlets' coverage as "FICTION and LIES." On September 19, 2026, the outlets' reporters were denied entry at the White House gates after their hard passes, the standing credentials that let reporters enter the White House press area without applying each day, were deactivated. The outlets sued on September 21, 2026, and the case is pending as of 2026-09-22.{c:1}
stated_justification: In his announcement on September 18, 2026, Trump described the outlets' coverage as "FICTION and LIES." The same day he told a Bloomberg reporter, "I dislike dishonest press, like you. I think you're terrible." The White House has not identified a specific story that prompted the decision (as of 2026-09-22).{c:106}
effect_on_reporting: Reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico can no longer enter the White House grounds with their hard passes, which were deactivated on September 19, 2026 (as of 2026-09-22). On September 20, 2026, the other networks in the White House press pool declined to fill CNN's rotating slot, so no replacement crew covered it for the shared pool feed that other outlets use.{c:3}
unknowns: The White House has not said which story or stories prompted the decision (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States: News organizations turn in their Pentagon press credentials, October 2025
outcome_note: Credentials were ordered restored for seven New York Times journalists on 2026-03-20; the ruling against the revised policy on 2026-04-09 is on appeal. Most other outlets remain outside the building.
summary: Beginning on October 15, 2025, reporters from at least 30 news organizations vacated the press workspace at the Pentagon, the headquarters of the United States Department of Defense, rather than sign the department's new credential pledge, with a deadline of October 17 to remove their belongings. They included ABC News, NBC News, CBS News, Fox News, CNN, the Associated Press, Reuters, Bloomberg News, The New York Times, The Washington Post, The Wall Street Journal, NPR and Politico. One America News Network said it would sign. As of 2026-09-22, most of these outlets cover the Pentagon from outside the building.{c:93}
stated_justification: The Department of Defense gave no separate reason for requiring the pledge as a condition of the badge. It described the underlying rules as "an important step in preventing leaks that damage operational security and national security."{c:5}{c:93}{c:94}
effect_on_reporting: Reporters from most major news organizations lost routine access to the Pentagon building and its press workspace, and cover the department from outside it (as of 2026-09-22).{c:5}

title: United States: White House takes over selection of the presidential press pool, February 2025
outcome_note: The White House selects the pool as of 2026-09-22, according to the Associated Press (s104).
summary: On February 25, 2025, the White House announced that it would decide which journalists join the press pool, the small rotating group of reporters who cover the president of the United States in spaces such as the Oval Office and Air Force One and share what they gather with other outlets. The White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA), the organization of reporters who cover the president, said that for more than a century "working journalists" and "not government officials" had "determined pool rotation procedures." As of 2026-09-22, the White House selects the pool, according to the Associated Press.{c:6}
stated_justification: The White House asserted its authority over access to spaces such as the Oval Office and Air Force One. It has not given a further reason for taking over pool selection (as of 2026-09-22).{c:6}{c:7}{c:95}
effect_on_reporting: The White House, rather than the working press corps, decides which outlets rotate into the pool that covers the president in small venues, and the pool has included outlets that were not part of the previous rotation (as of 2026-09-22).{c:7}

title: United States: Federal Communications Commission chairman's remarks and the suspension of Jimmy Kimmel Live!, September 2025
issue_of_the_day: Jimmy Kimmel's on-air remarks about speculation over the motives of the person who killed Charlie Kirk, according to NPR.
outcome_note: ABC announced the show's return for 2025-09-23 after about a week off the air, according to Al Jazeera (s112).
summary: On September 17, 2025, the chairman of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), the United States regulator of broadcasting, Brendan Carr, said broadcasters could "do this the easy way or the hard way" over remarks by the television host Jimmy Kimmel, and warned of "additional work for the FCC ahead." Within hours, the station owners Nexstar and Sinclair said they would pull Jimmy Kimmel Live! from their stations, and ABC, the network that airs it, did the same, according to NPR. ABC announced that the show would return on September 23, 2025, according to Al Jazeera.{c:96}
stated_justification: Carr said, "We can do this the easy way or the hard way. These companies can find ways to change conduct to take action on Kimmel or, you know, there's going to be additional work for the FCC ahead."{c:8}
effect_on_reporting: Jimmy Kimmel Live! went off the air on ABC and on stations owned by Nexstar and Sinclair from September 17, 2025, until ABC returned it to its schedule after "a weeklong impasse," according to Al Jazeera.{c:97}
unknowns: The FCC, ABC, Nexstar and Sinclair have not made public any private communications between them about the suspension (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States: Paramount settlement of Donald Trump's lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview, July 2025
issue_of_the_day: 60 Minutes' editing of a 2024 interview with Kamala Harris, then vice-president of the United States.
outcome_note: Settled on 2025-07-01: US$16 million to Trump's future presidential library and the plaintiffs' fees and costs; 60 Minutes to release transcripts of presidential-candidate interviews. The outcome enum has no value for a settlement; "sustained" records that the settlement terms stand.
summary: On July 1, 2025, Paramount, the parent company of the United States broadcaster CBS News, announced that it would settle for US$16 million a lawsuit brought by Donald Trump, the president of the United States, over how the CBS program 60 Minutes edited a 2024 interview with Kamala Harris, then vice-president. The money goes to Trump's future presidential library and the plaintiffs' fees and costs, and 60 Minutes will release transcripts of future interviews with presidential candidates, "subject to redactions as required for legal or national security concerns." Paramount "has maintained that the lawsuit was completely without merit," according to CBS News.{c:99}
stated_justification: Trump's lawsuit alleged that CBS aired two differently edited excerpts of the same answer from the Harris interview in a deceptive way. Paramount "has maintained that the lawsuit was completely without merit," according to CBS News.{c:9}
effect_on_reporting: Under the settlement announced on July 1, 2025, 60 Minutes will release transcripts of its interviews with presidential candidates, "subject to redactions as required for legal or national security concerns."{c:100}
unknowns: Paramount has not said whether its pending merger with Skydance Media, which awaited approval from United States regulators, bore on its decision to settle (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States: U.S. Agency for Global Media action to shut down Voice of America operations, March 2025
outcome_note: A temporary restraining order of 2025-03-28 barred USAGM from reducing its workforce; litigation continued into 2026.
summary: Beginning on March 15, 2025, the U.S. Agency for Global Media (USAGM), the United States federal agency that oversees the government's international broadcasters, placed most of its staff on paid administrative leave and moved to shut down the operations of Voice of America (VOA), the United States government's international broadcaster. Kari Lake, a senior advisor at USAGM, carried out the action under an executive order of the president of the United States, Donald Trump, to reduce the federal bureaucracy. VOA journalists sued on March 21, 2025, and on March 28, 2025, a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order, a short-term order made before a full hearing, that barred the agency from reducing its workforce.{c:40}
stated_justification: USAGM said it was complying with the executive order to "reduce the federal bureaucracy" and cutting costs, including by cancelling what it called an "obscenely expensive 15-year lease."{c:41}
effect_on_reporting: VOA broadcasts to audiences in countries including Iran, China and Russia were interrupted, and hundreds of journalists were placed on leave or laid off.{c:42}
unknowns: The sources cited do not state the final outcome of the lawsuit or USAGM's long-term staffing plan for VOA (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States: Department of Justice rescission of rules limiting subpoenas of journalists, April 2025
outcome_note: In effect since 2025-04-25; the sources cited report no restoration of the earlier rules (as of 2026-09-22).
summary: On April 25, 2025, the Attorney General of the United States, Pam Bondi, head of the Department of Justice, the federal department that prosecutes federal crimes, rescinded rules adopted in 2021 and 2022 under her predecessor, Merrick Garland, that barred prosecutors from seeking reporters' records or testimony to identify the sources of leaks. Bondi's memo said leaks of sensitive information to the media undermine the department's ability "to uphold the rule of law, protect civil rights, and keep America safe." The department returned to a test that weighs law enforcement interests against press freedom, according to the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, a United States non-profit that provides legal help to journalists.{c:102}
stated_justification: A Department of Justice memo said, "Federal government employees intentionally leaking sensitive information to the media undermines the ability of the Department of Justice to uphold the rule of law, protect civil rights, and keep America safe."{c:10}
effect_on_reporting: Journalists who cover national security and law enforcement in the United States can again be subpoenaed for records or compelled to testify in leak investigations, which the 2021 and 2022 rules had been written to prevent.{c:11}
unknowns: The sources cited do not state whether the Department of Justice has subpoenaed a journalist under the restored balancing test (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States: White House suspension of CNN correspondent Jim Acosta's hard pass, November 2018
issue_of_the_day: An exchange between Acosta and Trump at a White House news conference on November 7, 2018, after the United States midterm elections.
outcome_note: A temporary restraining order of 2018-11-16 required reinstatement; the White House restored the pass on 2018-11-19 and CNN dropped the suit.
summary: On November 7, 2018, the White House suspended the hard pass of CNN's White House correspondent, Jim Acosta, after what Gulf News called a "heated confrontation" between Acosta and the president of the United States, Donald Trump, at a news conference after the country's midterm elections. A hard pass is the standing credential that lets a reporter enter the White House press area without applying each day. On November 16, 2018, a federal judge granted CNN a temporary restraining order requiring the pass to be reinstated, and the White House restored it on November 19, 2018, after which CNN dropped its lawsuit.{c:46}
stated_justification: The White House said Acosta had placed his hands on "a young woman just trying to do her job as a White House intern" when she tried to take the microphone from him. CNN disputed that account.{c:47}
effect_on_reporting: Acosta could not enter the White House grounds with his hard pass from November 7 to November 19, 2018. After the case, the White House issued its first written rules for reporters' conduct at news conferences.{c:44}

title: United States (Louisiana): 25-foot buffer zone law around police officers, May 2024
outcome_note: Enforcement blocked by a preliminary injunction on 2025-01-31 while the case is pending; Louisiana's appeal was reported pending as of mid-2026.
summary: On May 28, 2024, the governor of Louisiana, a state in the southern United States, Jeff Landry, signed a law that makes it a crime to stay within 25 feet (about 7.6 metres) of a working law enforcement officer after the officer has told a person to step back. The law applies to everyone, including journalists. Supporters described it as protecting officers' safety while they work. On January 31, 2025, a federal judge blocked its enforcement while a challenge to it is decided.{c:110}
stated_justification: Supporters described the law as protecting officers' safety while they perform their duties. Landry said on signing it, "This is part of our continued pledge to address public safety."{c:49}
effect_on_reporting: Journalists and others filming police in Louisiana had to stay at least 25 feet (7.6 metres) away once warned, or face jail, until a federal judge blocked enforcement on January 31, 2025.{c:50}

title: United States (Florida): Halo Law buffer zone around first responders, January 2025
outcome_note: In effect from 2025-01-01; the sources cited report no court order blocking it (as of 2026-09-22).
summary: On January 1, 2025, the "Halo Law" took effect in Florida, a state in the south-eastern United States. It creates a 25-foot (7.6-metre) buffer zone around first responders, such as police officers, firefighters and paramedics, while they are performing their duties, and anyone who enters the zone "to 'harass, impede or threaten' first responders after receiving a warning" faces up to 60 days in prison and a fine of US$500. The law applies to journalists as well as the public. The governor of Florida, Ron DeSantis, signed it in 2024.{c:55}
stated_justification: The law was presented as protecting first responders at active scenes. It applies "anywhere that first responders are actively performing their duties by creating a 25-foot buffer zone to allow them to carry on their duties," according to Fire Law Blog.{c:56}
effect_on_reporting: Journalists covering police, fire and ambulance services in Florida must keep a 25-foot (7.6-metre) distance once warned, which limits their ability to document first responders' conduct at close range.{c:57}
unknowns: The sources cited do not state whether the Halo Law has been challenged in court (as of 2026-09-22).

title: Israel: ban on independent entry of foreign journalists into the Gaza Strip, 2023 to 2026
issue_of_the_day: The war in Gaza, which began in October 2023.
outcome_note: In effect as of CPJ's report of 2026-02-25; the government asked Israel's Supreme Court in January 2026 to keep the ban.
summary: Since the war in Gaza began in October 2023, the government of Israel has barred foreign journalists from entering the Gaza Strip, the Palestinian territory on the Mediterranean coast between Israel and Egypt, independently; foreign correspondents have entered only on trips escorted by the Israeli military. On January 7, 2026, Al Jazeera reported that the Foreign Press Association, which represents journalists from international news organizations, had condemned the government's decision to keep the ban. The government had told Israel's Supreme Court that the ban should be maintained due to "security reasons," according to Al Jazeera. On February 25, 2026, the Committee to Protect Journalists reported that the ban was still in place.{c:113}
stated_justification: Israeli authorities have cited military security concerns for restricting the movement of foreign journalists in Gaza. In January 2026, the government told Israel's Supreme Court that the ban should be maintained due to "security reasons" and that its position was "based on the position of the defence establishment," according to Al Jazeera.{c:105}{c:112}{c:113}
effect_on_reporting: International coverage of Gaza has relied on Palestinian journalists working inside the territory, rather than on foreign correspondents reporting independently.{c:112}
unknowns: The sources cited do not state whether Israel's Supreme Court has ruled on the Foreign Press Association's petition (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States: White House exclusion of the Associated Press from the Oval Office and Air Force One, February 2025
issue_of_the_day: AP's continued use of the name "Gulf of Mexico" after an executive order of the president of the United States renamed the body of water the "Gulf of America" for federal purposes.
outcome_note: The D.C. Circuit's partial stay of 2025-06-06 keeps AP out of the Oval Office, Air Force One, Mar-a-Lago and the Cabinet Room and admits it to the East Room; the full court denied rehearing en banc on 2025-07-22. The appeal is pending.
summary: On February 16, 2025, the White House, the office of the president of the United States, began barring journalists from the Associated Press (AP), a United States news agency, from the Oval Office and Air Force One, the aircraft that carries the president. The exclusion followed AP's decision to keep using the name "Gulf of Mexico" after an executive order of the president, Donald Trump, renamed the body of water the "Gulf of America" for United States federal purposes. Trump told reporters, "We're going to keep them out until such time as they agree that it's the Gulf of America," according to NPR. AP sued on February 21, 2025; as of 2026-09-22, a partial stay by a federal appeals court leaves AP excluded from the Oval Office and Air Force One.{c:108}
stated_justification: Trump told reporters in February 2025, "We're going to keep them out until such time as they agree that it's the Gulf of America," according to NPR. The White House tied AP's access to its use of the name set by the executive order.{c:29}
effect_on_reporting: AP reporters and photographers lost access to the Oval Office and Air Force One, small spaces where the news agency had held a regular place in the rotating press pool that covers the president. Trump and his aides barred AP's White House reporters from "dozens of events since February," including events limited to the pool, according to NPR.{c:30}

title: United States: Department of Defense press credential rules requiring approval before release of information, September 2025
outcome_note: Judge Paul Friedman ruled against the credential-revocation provisions on 2026-03-20 and against the revised policy on 2026-04-09; the Department of Defense appealed.
summary: On September 21, 2025, the United States Department of Defense, the federal department that provides the country's military forces, issued new credential rules for reporters at the Pentagon, its headquarters building, under the Secretary of Defense, Pete Hegseth. The rules require that information be approved for public release by an authorizing official "before it is released, even if it is unclassified," and require accredited reporters to pledge not to solicit or publish such information without approval or lose their badges. The Pentagon called the rules "an important step in preventing leaks that damage operational security and national security." A federal judge ruled against the rules in March and April 2026, and the department has appealed (as of 2026-09-22).{c:109}
stated_justification: The Department of Defense said the rules were "an important step in preventing leaks that damage operational security and national security."{c:33}
effect_on_reporting: Reporters who declined to sign the pledge lost their Pentagon credentials and building access. Reporters who sign may not solicit or publish sensitive unclassified information unless a Pentagon official has approved its release.{c:34}
unknowns: The Department of Defense has not published a list of what counts as "sensitive but unclassified" information under the rules (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States: Executive Order 14290 directing an end to federal funding for NPR and PBS, May 2025
outcome_note: No court ruling on Executive Order 14290 and no final funding figure appears in the sources cited (as of 2026-09-22).
summary: On May 1, 2025, the president of the United States, Donald Trump, signed Executive Order 14290, "Ending Taxpayer Subsidization of Biased Media." It directs the Corporation for Public Broadcasting (CPB), a private non-profit corporation created by the United States Congress in 1967 to distribute federal money to public radio and television, and federal agencies to stop funding NPR and PBS, the country's non-profit public radio and television networks. The order says public funding for news is "not only outdated and unnecessary but corrosive to the appearance of journalistic independence." NPR and PBS said the president cannot cut funding that Congress has appropriated to CPB.{c:36}
stated_justification: The order says public funding for news programming is "not only outdated and unnecessary but corrosive to the appearance of journalistic independence." The accompanying White House fact sheet said, "Neither entity presents a fair, accurate or unbiased portrayal of current events to tax-paying citizens."{c:37}
effect_on_reporting: The order directs CPB and federal agencies to stop funding NPR and PBS, whose member stations include smaller rural and tribal stations that rely most heavily on CPB grants for their operating budgets.{c:38}
unknowns: The sources cited do not state the order's effect in dollars on individual member stations or the outcome of NPR's and PBS's legal response (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States (Louisiana): Federal court order blocking enforcement of the police buffer zone law, January 2025
outcome_note: Preliminary injunction granted 2025-01-31; Louisiana's appeal was reported pending as of mid-2026.
summary: On January 31, 2025, Judge John W. deGravelles of the United States District Court for the Middle District of Louisiana, a federal trial court, blocked enforcement of the state's 25-foot (7.6-metre) police buffer zone law with a preliminary injunction, an order that keeps the situation as it is while a case is decided. He wrote that "the distance required is likely to impede Plaintiffs' non-obstructive newsgathering" and that "the Act has a chilling effect on Plaintiffs' First Amendment rights." The plaintiffs included journalists and civil rights observers. Louisiana was reported to be appealing the order.{c:52}
stated_justification: Louisiana defended the law in court as an officer-safety measure.{c:52}{c:53}{c:54}
effect_on_reporting: While the injunction is in place, journalists and the public in Louisiana may film police from ordinary distances.{c:53}
unknowns: No ruling on Louisiana's appeal appears in the sources cited (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States: Nixon White House "enemies list" naming journalists, September 1971
outcome_note: No ruling or formal rescission applies; the lists became public during the Watergate investigations of 1973 to 1974.
summary: On September 9, 1971, the office of Charles Colson, special counsel to the president of the United States, Richard Nixon, sent White House Counsel John Dean, the president's lawyer on official matters, a memorandum naming 20 people as an initial "enemies list." The list named political opponents, including journalists, for possible action through federal agencies, such as tax audits by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), the United States federal tax agency. The IRS commissioner, Donald C. Alexander, refused to launch audits of the people on the list. The lists became public during the Watergate investigations into Nixon's White House.{c:59}
stated_justification: No public justification was issued. An internal White House memo by Dean described the purpose as "how we can use the available federal machinery to screw our political enemies."{c:60}
effect_on_reporting: Journalists named on the list faced possible federal scrutiny, including tax audits. The IRS did not carry out the audits on the people listed.{c:61}
unknowns: The sources cited do not give the complete roster of journalists on every version of the list, or whether any individual reporter was audited because of it.

title: United States: Espionage Act prosecutions of sources for leaks to the press, 2009 to 2013
outcome_note: The record documents the prosecutions as a group; the outcome of each case is not recorded here.
summary: A report by the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), a non-profit organization in New York that documents cases of journalists imprisoned or killed worldwide, published on October 10, 2013, found that since 2009 the United States Department of Justice had brought felony charges against six government employees and two contractors, including Edward Snowden, accused of leaking classified information to the press. The charges were brought under the Espionage Act, a 1917 United States law against disclosing defence information, during the presidency of Barack Obama. The Project On Government Oversight, a United States non-profit that investigates the federal government, said the department under Obama and Attorney General Eric Holder "has used it more than all prior administrations combined."{c:63}
stated_justification: The prosecutions were brought case by case on national security grounds, not under one stated policy. Matthew Miller, then spokesman for Attorney General Eric Holder, told the report's author, "It was never a conscious decision to bring more of these cases than we ever had. It was a combination of things."{c:64}
effect_on_reporting: Journalists and their sources in national security reporting said they avoided contact by phone or email for fear of being identified through records requests, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists.{c:65}

title: Hungary: National Sovereignty Protection Act and Sovereignty Protection Office, December 2023
outcome_note: The National Assembly abolished the Sovereignty Protection Office on 2026-06-30, according to CPJ (s055).
summary: On December 20, 2023, the president of Hungary, Katalin Novák, promulgated the National Sovereignty Protection Act, passed by the National Assembly, Hungary's parliament, during the government of the prime minister, Viktor Orbán. The law created a Sovereignty Protection Office empowered to investigate organizations, including news outlets, that it determined might be influenced by foreign actors or threaten national sovereignty. A week earlier, ten Hungarian media outlets had said the law "is capable of severely restricting the freedom of the press." After a change of government in 2026, the National Assembly abolished the office on June 30, 2026.{c:67}
stated_justification: The law's sponsors presented it as protecting Hungary's national sovereignty against foreign influence over civil society and the media. Novák said the office would comply with Hungary's Basic Law, its constitution, and have no impact on press freedom, according to RSF.{c:68}
effect_on_reporting: Hungarian news outlets that receive foreign funding could be investigated by the Sovereignty Protection Office from December 2023 until its abolition on June 30, 2026. CPJ wrote in July 2026 that the office "had been used to harass and delegitimize independent media by labeling them threats to national sovereignty."{c:69}

title: India: one-year prison sentence for the journalist Ravi Nair in a criminal defamation case, February 2026
outcome_note: Sentenced on 2026-02-10; no appeal or ruling on appeal appears in the sources cited.
summary: On February 10, 2026, a court in India sentenced the investigative journalist Ravi Nair to one year in prison and a fine of 5,000 rupees (about US$55) for criminal defamation, an offence under which a statement that damages someone's reputation can lead to a fine or prison sentence. The case concerned posts on the platform X between October 2020 and July 2021 and articles on Adani Watch, an Australian non-profit investigative site, that criticized the Adani Group, an Indian conglomerate. CIVICUS Monitor, which tracks civic freedoms by country, recorded the sentence among arrests, detentions and police summonses of Indian journalists in the same period.{c:71}
stated_justification: The case was a criminal defamation prosecution over Nair's published statements about the Adani Group. The sources cited record no statement of reason from the government of India.{c:71}{c:72}{c:73}
effect_on_reporting: Nair faces a year in prison over his posts and articles about the Adani Group (as of February 2026). CIVICUS wrote that in India "sedition and anti-terror laws were used to criminalise journalists, comedians, academics and students exercising their right to freedom of expression."{c:72}
unknowns: The sources cited do not state whether Nair has appealed, or which court sentenced him (as of 2026-09-22).

title: Russia: law on asset freezes and service denials for exiled "foreign agents", August 2026
outcome_note: Signed and in force on 2026-08-04, according to RSF (s062).
summary: On August 4, 2026, the president of Russia, Vladimir Putin, signed a law, adopted unanimously by the Russian parliament on July 24, 2026, that allows the authorities to freeze bank accounts, block property and vehicle sales and deny consular services such as passport renewal to Russians in exile who have been designated "foreign agents" or who cooperate with organizations Russia has labelled "undesirable." A "foreign agent" is a Russian legal designation that places a person or organization on a government register and subjects them to added restrictions. Of those designated, "the vast majority are journalists," according to Reporters Without Borders (RSF). The law entered into force the same day.{c:74}
stated_justification: The sources cited give no official reason for the law beyond Russia's "foreign agent" and "undesirable organization" framework, in place since 2012. RSF and Freedom House describe that framework as treating independent and exiled media as instruments of foreign influence.{c:77}
effect_on_reporting: Exiled Russian journalists designated "foreign agents" can lose access to their bank accounts, their right to sell property and consular services such as passport renewal (as of 2026-08-04).{c:75}

title: El Salvador: freeze on assets of shareholders in El Faro's parent company, February to April 2026
outcome_note: In place as reported by CPJ on 2026-05-08; no reversal is reported in the sources cited.
summary: Between February and April 2026, the government of El Salvador, headed by the president, Nayib Bukele, placed "preventative annotations" on a bank account and real estate belonging to two partners of Trípode S.A. de C.V., the parent company of the investigative news outlet El Faro, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), a non-profit organization in New York. CPJ said on May 8, 2026 that "the targeting of individual shareholders' personal assets marks a dangerous escalation in the Bukele administration's long-standing effort to dismantle El Faro through administrative harassment." The sources cited give no public reason from the Salvadoran government for the measure.{c:78}
stated_justification: The Salvadoran government has not given a public reason for the freeze in the sources cited (as of 2026-05-08). The Bukele administration has described earlier actions affecting critical outlets in terms of tax and regulatory compliance.{c:81}
effect_on_reporting: Two partners in El Faro's parent company had a bank account and real estate placed under "preventative annotations," adding personal financial pressure to years of administrative and legal pressure that CPJ and RSF say has pushed Salvadoran journalists into exile.{c:79}
unknowns: The sources cited do not state the legal basis Salvadoran authorities gave for the freeze (as of 2026-09-22).

title: China (Hong Kong): conviction and 20-year sentence of the media owner Jimmy Lai under the National Security Law, 2025 to 2026
outcome_note: Sentenced to 20 years in prison on 2026-02-08; no appeal is recorded in the sources cited.
summary: On December 15, 2025, the High Court of Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China with its own courts, convicted Jimmy Lai, founder of the newspaper Apple Daily, on two counts of "conspiracy to commit collusion with foreign forces" under the National Security Law, which China's central government imposed on Hong Kong in 2020, and one count of "conspiracy to publish seditious publications." On February 8, 2026, the court sentenced Lai to 20 years in prison. Apple Daily shut down in June 2021 after its accounts were frozen and much of its top leadership was arrested. Human Rights Watch, an international human rights organization, called the charges "bogus."{c:111}
stated_justification: Hong Kong prosecutors alleged that Lai conspired with foreign forces and published seditious material through Apple Daily, and the authorities treated the case as a national security matter under the 2020 law. The court ruled that Lai was the "mastermind" of the alleged conspiracies in all three counts.{c:83}
effect_on_reporting: Apple Daily and Next Magazine no longer publish. Apple Daily shut down in June 2021 after its accounts were frozen and much of its top leadership was arrested.{c:84}
unknowns: The sources cited do not state whether Lai has appealed (as of 2026-09-22).

title: Türkiye: detention, injury and deportation of journalists covering protests, March 2025
issue_of_the_day: The detention of the mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem İmamoğlu, on March 19, 2025, and the protests that followed.
outcome_note: CPJ's report of 2025-04-02 describes the restrictions as continuing; the outcomes for individual journalists are not recorded.
summary: After the detention of the mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem İmamoğlu, on March 19, 2025, protests spread in Türkiye, and between March 19 and March 28, 2025, the authorities detained at least 13 journalists, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), a non-profit organization in New York. From March 21 to 23, 2025, at least 14 journalists were injured after being beaten or shot with rubber bullets by Istanbul police, and on March 27 police detained the BBC correspondent Mark Lowen and deported him. CPJ said on April 2, 2025 that the authorities "have since arrested thousands of protesters and have moved aggressively to tamp down media coverage."{c:86}
stated_justification: The authorities cited "accusations of corruption" against Istanbul's municipal government, controlled by the opposition Republican People's Party (CHP), as the basis for the action against İmamoğlu. The sources cited give no separate reason for the detentions of journalists.{c:87}
effect_on_reporting: Journalists covering the protests were detained, injured or, in Lowen's case, deported between March 19 and March 28, 2025, which reduced on-the-ground coverage of the demonstrations and their policing.{c:88}
unknowns: The sources cited do not give the legal outcome for each detained journalist (as of 2026-09-22).

title: United States postmaster bars the magazine The Masses from the mail under the Espionage Act
issue_of_the_day: The United States had entered the First World War three months earlier and introduced a military draft. The Masses had run cartoons and articles opposing the war and conscription, which the Post Office treated as material likely to obstruct recruiting.
outcome_note: The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed Judge Hand's order later in 1917, and the Post Office's mail ban on The Masses stood.
summary: Weeks after the United States entered the First World War, the New York postmaster used the new Espionage Act, a law against interfering with military recruitment, to bar the socialist magazine The Masses from the mail. A judge's order protecting the magazine was reversed on appeal.{c:114}{c:115}{c:116}
what_happened: Congress passed the Espionage Act in June 1917, a law that made it a crime to interfere with military recruitment or operations during the First World War. New York's postmaster, Thomas Patten, used the act to declare the August 1917 issue of The Masses, an anti-war socialist magazine, unmailable because of its cartoons and articles opposing the war and the draft. The magazine asked the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, the federal trial court covering Manhattan, to block the ban. Judge Learned Hand agreed, ruling that the magazine's writers had criticized the war without directly urging readers to break the law. The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, the appeals court above Hand's, reversed him months later, and the mail ban stood. The Post Office went on to deny mailing privileges to dozens more anti-war and socialist publications under the same law.{c:114}{c:115}{c:116}
stated_justification: Postmaster Patten found the magazine's cartoons and articles likely, in the language of the Espionage Act, to cause insubordination in the armed forces and to obstruct recruiting.{c:114}
effect_on_reporting: The Masses lost the low second-class postal rate that let it reach subscribers across the country and stopped publishing within months; dozens of other anti-war and socialist papers lost mailing privileges the same way.{c:116}

title: United States Postmaster General Burleson strips the Milwaukee Leader of its mailing rate
issue_of_the_day: The Leader had published articles criticizing United States participation in the First World War and the draft, which the Post Office treated as violations of the Espionage Act's ban on obstructing military recruitment.
outcome_note: The Supreme Court upheld the revocation of the Leader's mailing rate 7 to 2 in United States ex rel. Milwaukee Social Democratic Publishing Co. v. Burleson.
summary: Postmaster General Albert Burleson used the wartime Espionage Act to strip the Milwaukee Leader, a socialist daily, of its low-cost second-class mailing rate, cutting off its main channel to readers. The Supreme Court upheld the revocation in 1921, over two dissents warning it amounted to press controls.{c:117}{c:118}{c:119}
what_happened: During the First World War, Postmaster General Albert Burleson's Post Office found the Milwaukee Leader, a socialist daily edited under publisher Victor Berger's direction, in violation of the Espionage Act for articles opposing the war, and revoked its second-class mailing permit, the low postal rate newspapers depended on to reach subscribers nationwide. The paper's publishing company asked the Supreme Court of the United States, the country's highest court, to order the Post Office to restore the rate, arguing the denial violated the Constitution's protections for speech and due process. In United States ex rel. Milwaukee Social Democratic Publishing Co. v. Burleson, decided March 7, 1921, the Court upheld Burleson's action by a 7 to 2 vote. Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes and Louis Brandeis dissented, warning that letting a postmaster judge a paper's loyalty amounted to a form of press controls over the mail.{c:117}{c:118}{c:119}
stated_justification: The Post Office found the Leader's wartime articles violated the Espionage Act, and the majority opinion held that the Constitution was not a shield for those who used its privileges to work against the government.{c:117}
effect_on_reporting: The Leader lost the inexpensive second-class postal rate other newspapers used to reach subscribers across the country, forcing it onto costlier first-class postage and cutting its circulation.{c:118}

title: United States Supreme Court strikes down a Minnesota law used to shut a newspaper
issue_of_the_day: The Saturday Press had run articles accusing Minneapolis officials, police and a local gangster of corruption and racketeering, allegations the county attorney treated as scandalous and defamatory under the state's 1925 nuisance law.
outcome_note: The Supreme Court of the United States struck down the Minnesota law 5 to 4 as a restraint on publication in advance that the Constitution did not allow.
summary: A Hennepin County attorney used Minnesota's 1925 Public Nuisance Law to shut down The Saturday Press, a Minneapolis paper accusing officials of corruption. In 1931 the Supreme Court of the United States struck the law down, ruling that stopping a paper before publication was itself a form of press controls.{c:120}{c:121}{c:122}
what_happened: Minnesota's 1925 Public Nuisance Law let a judge permanently shut any newspaper or periodical found to be malicious, scandalous or defamatory. In 1927 the Hennepin County Attorney, Floyd Olson, used the law to close The Saturday Press, a Minneapolis weekly run by Jay Near that had accused local officials and gangsters of corruption. Near appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States, the country's highest court, arguing the law violated the free-press guarantee that the First Amendment applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment's due process clause. On June 1, 1931, the Court ruled 5 to 4 in Near v. Minnesota that the law amounted to a prior restraint the Constitution did not allow, meaning government could not stop publication in advance, even of material later found libelous; a publisher could still be sued afterward, but the paper itself could not be shut down first. The decision became the foundation of later United States rulings against government orders blocking publication before it happens.{c:120}{c:121}{c:122}
stated_justification: Minnesota officials said the Public Nuisance Law applied to papers that habitually published malicious, scandalous or defamatory material, and treated The Saturday Press's allegations against local officials as exactly that kind of publication.{c:121}
effect_on_reporting: The Saturday Press was shut down under the injunction; after the Supreme Court's ruling, states lost the power to close a newspaper in advance for its content, though publishers remained open to being sued afterward.{c:122}

title: United States creates an Office of Censorship and a wartime code for the press
issue_of_the_day: The United States had just entered the Second World War after the Japanese bombing of Pearl Harbor, and the government wanted to prevent newspapers and broadcasters from unintentionally publishing information useful to enemy forces.
outcome_note: The Office of Censorship operated on the press's voluntary compliance through the war and was abolished by executive order after Japan's surrender.
summary: Twelve days after the bombing of Pearl Harbor, President Franklin Roosevelt created the Office of Censorship. Its director, Byron Price, a former Associated Press editor, wrote a Code of Wartime Practices asking newspapers and broadcasters to withhold information such as troop movements, and most of the press followed it voluntarily.{c:125}
what_happened: Twelve days after Japan's December 7, 1941 bombing of the United States naval base at Pearl Harbor drew the country into the Second World War, President Franklin Roosevelt signed an order on December 19, 1941 creating the Office of Censorship. He named Byron Price, a former executive news editor of the Associated Press wire service, to run it. Price's office wrote a Code of Wartime Practices for American newspapers and, separately, for radio stations, asking editors and broadcasters not to publish or air information of possible use to an enemy, such as troop, ship and plane movements, weather conditions, casualty lists and damage to military targets. The code was voluntary rather than a legal requirement, and American publishers and broadcasters, largely supportive of the war effort, followed it without a formal enforcement mechanism. The office also opened and read international mail, cables and other communications. It was abolished once the war in the Pacific ended.{c:123}{c:124}{c:125}
stated_justification: Roosevelt said Americans hated press controls as much as they hated war but treated it as unavoidable in wartime, arguing that military information of possible use to an enemy had to be kept from publication at its source.{c:123}
effect_on_reporting: Newspapers and broadcasters voluntarily withheld reporting on troop and ship movements, fortifications, weather, casualty lists and damage to military targets for the war's duration under the Office of Censorship's code.{c:124}

title: United States Senate panel subpoenas dozens of New York Times journalists over Communist ties
issue_of_the_day: Senator Eastland's subcommittee was investigating what it described as Communist Party influence in American newsrooms and broadcasting during the Cold War, and treated past party membership among journalists as grounds for scrutiny.
outcome_note: The dismissals and resignations at The New York Times and other papers were not reversed; the paper said at year's end it had made no further dismissals beyond the initial cases.
summary: The Senate Internal Security Subcommittee, led by Senator James Eastland, issued 35 subpoenas over past or present Communist Party ties in the press, and 26 of them went to New York Times staff. The newspaper protested but several employees who would not answer were fired or forced to resign.{c:126}{c:127}{c:128}
what_happened: The Senate Internal Security Subcommittee, a Senate panel investigating Communist Party influence chaired by Senator James Eastland of Mississippi, issued a wave of subpoenas in November 1955 for closed hearings on Communism in the press, radio and television industries. Of 35 subpoenas issued, 26 went to past or present employees of The New York Times. The newspaper's own editorial page said the investigation appeared aimed squarely at the paper, while also saying it did not believe in permanent guilt and thought employees could make up for past association with the Communist Party through good work. Even so, several Times staff members who indicated they would invoke their Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination rather than answer the subcommittee's questions were dismissed or pressured to resign before or after testifying, including one employee let go before the hearings even began. Other newspapers, including the New York Daily News and the Hearst-owned Daily Mirror, fired staff members in the same way.{c:126}{c:127}{c:128}
stated_justification: The Senate Internal Security Subcommittee said it was investigating Communist Party influence within newsrooms, and its subpoenas asked witnesses about past or present party membership.{c:127}
effect_on_reporting: Journalists at The New York Times and other papers who would not answer the subcommittee's questions about Communist Party ties were fired or pressured into resigning, a pattern that spread to other newsrooms during the hearings.{c:128}

title: Nixon White House compiles an enemies list naming journalists for official pressure
issue_of_the_day: Nixon's aides were reacting to sustained critical coverage and commentary from named journalists during his first term, including Mary McGrory's columns, which an internal notation described as habitually critical to the president.
outcome_note: The list became public during John Dean's Senate Watergate Committee testimony, discrediting the effort as Nixon's presidency unraveled over the wider Watergate scandal.
summary: White House Counsel John Dean wrote a memo on how to use federal agencies against President Nixon's political opponents, and the resulting list of more than 200 names included journalists such as CBS News correspondent Daniel Schorr. It became public during the 1973 Senate Watergate hearings.{c:129}{c:130}{c:131}
what_happened: Staff in President Richard Nixon's White House began compiling a list of political opponents in June 1971. On August 16, 1971, White House Counsel John Dean wrote a memo titled 'Dealing with our Political Enemies,' describing how the administration could use the machinery of the federal government, including the Internal Revenue Service, the United States tax-collection agency, to conduct tax audits and other scrutiny of people and organizations it considered critical. The list grew to more than 200 names by September 1971 and included a media category naming journalists alongside politicians, activists and business figures. CBS News correspondent Daniel Schorr discovered he was number 17 on the list; The Washington Post columnist Mary McGrory was included for what an internal notation called her 'daily hate Nixon articles.' Dean revealed the list during his testimony to the Senate Watergate Committee, the Senate panel investigating the Watergate scandal, on June 27, 1973, making it public for the first time.{c:129}{c:130}{c:131}
stated_justification: Dean's memo described the effort as a way to use the available machinery of the federal government against people the administration regarded as its political enemies, without citing any specific conduct by the journalists named.{c:129}
effect_on_reporting: Journalists named on the list, including Daniel Schorr and Mary McGrory, learned their reporting or commentary had made them targets for the same federal pressure, including possible tax audits, that the administration considered using against other political opponents.{c:130}

title: United States government seeks an injunction to stop The New York Times publishing the Pentagon Papers
issue_of_the_day: The Pentagon Papers documented decades of internal government decision-making on the Vietnam War that contradicted public statements by several administrations, and the Nixon administration sought to prevent further disclosure of the classified history.
outcome_note: The Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that the government's request for an injunction against publication failed to overcome the heavy presumption against prior restraint.
summary: After The New York Times began publishing a leaked secret history of the Vietnam War, the Nixon administration obtained a court order stopping further publication, the first such order against a major American newspaper. The Supreme Court lifted it two weeks later, ruling the government had not justified blocking publication in advance.{c:134}
what_happened: Military analyst Daniel Ellsberg copied a classified Defense Department history of United States involvement in Vietnam, later known as the Pentagon Papers, and gave it to The New York Times, which began publishing excerpts on June 13, 1971. The Department of Justice obtained a temporary restraining order from a federal court on June 15, 1971, the first time the United States government had gone to court to stop a major newspaper from publishing a specific story, arguing publication would harm national security. When The Washington Post also began publishing excerpts, the government sought an injunction against it too. The Supreme Court of the United States, the country's highest court, heard the consolidated case on an emergency basis and ruled 6 to 3 on June 30, 1971, in New York Times Co. v. United States, that the government had not met the heavy burden required to justify stopping publication in advance, and both papers resumed publishing.{c:132}{c:133}{c:134}
stated_justification: Government lawyers argued that publishing the classified history would cause grave and irreparable harm to United States national security and ongoing diplomatic and military efforts in Vietnam.{c:133}
effect_on_reporting: The New York Times and The Washington Post were barred by court order from publishing further excerpts of the Pentagon Papers for roughly two weeks until the Supreme Court lifted the injunction.{c:132}{c:133}{c:134}

title: United States Supreme Court rules reporters have no privilege to refuse grand jury subpoenas
issue_of_the_day: Branzburg's articles on drug use and manufacturing drew the attention of Kentucky prosecutors, who wanted him to identify the people he had described witnessing commit the underlying offenses.
outcome_note: The Supreme Court upheld the grand jury's power to compel Branzburg's testimony 5 to 4, finding no First Amendment reporter's privilege.
summary: Louisville Courier-Journal reporter Paul Branzburg was subpoenaed by a Kentucky grand jury, a body that investigates possible crimes, after he wrote about drug users he had observed. The Supreme Court ruled in 1972 that the First Amendment gives reporters no special right to withhold sources or information from a grand jury.{c:135}{c:136}{c:137}
what_happened: Paul Branzburg, a reporter for the Louisville Courier-Journal newspaper in Kentucky, wrote articles describing drug users he had observed making and using hashish, without naming them. A Jefferson County, Kentucky grand jury, a body of citizens that investigates possible crimes and can compel testimony, subpoenaed Branzburg in 1969 to identify the people he had written about; he refused, arguing the First Amendment protected him from having to reveal confidential sources and information gathered for reporting. His case was combined with two others raising the same question and reached the Supreme Court of the United States, the country's highest court. On June 29, 1972, the Court ruled 5 to 4 in Branzburg v. Hayes that reporters have the same obligation as any other citizen to answer relevant questions before a grand jury, rejecting the claim of a constitutional reporter's privilege to withhold sources.{c:135}{c:136}{c:137}
stated_justification: The Kentucky grand jury said it needed Branzburg's testimony to investigate the drug offenses he had personally witnessed while reporting, and the Supreme Court's majority held reporters had the same duty as other citizens to answer such questions.{c:136}
effect_on_reporting: Reporters in the United States gained no constitutional shield against being compelled to testify before a grand jury or reveal confidential sources, leaving protection for sources to depend on state shield laws or prosecutorial discretion.{c:137}

title: United States military bars journalists from the invasion of Grenada
issue_of_the_day: Defense officials had for years blamed unrestricted press coverage for damaging public and political support during the Vietnam War, and applied that lesson by excluding reporters from the opening phase of the Grenada operation.
outcome_note: The Pentagon created a standing national media pool in 1985 on the Sidle Commission's recommendation, formally reversing the total exclusion used in Grenada.
summary: When United States forces invaded the Caribbean island of Grenada on October 25, 1983, military commanders kept all journalists away from the island for the first two days of fighting, citing operational reasons. Protests from news organizations led the Pentagon to create a rotating press pool for future operations.{c:138}{c:139}{c:140}
what_happened: United States forces invaded the eastern Caribbean island nation of Grenada on October 25, 1983, under the Reagan administration, in an operation named Urgent Fury. Admiral Wesley McDonald, the operation's commander, barred journalists from the island for what he called operational reasons, and the Pentagon arranged no transportation, movement or communications facilities for reporters trying to reach Grenada on their own. Journalists were held on the nearby island of Barbados for roughly 48 hours while the fighting continued. After protests from news organizations and members of Congress, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the senior body of United States military leadership, ordered limited press access restored by October 28. The exclusion prompted a Pentagon-appointed panel, the Sidle Commission, to recommend a rotating pool of reporters for the early stages of future military operations, a system the Pentagon adopted in 1985.{c:138}{c:139}{c:140}
stated_justification: Military commanders said the initial exclusion of journalists protected reporters' safety during active combat, a rationale journalists disputed by noting they had always accepted the risks of covering war as part of their profession.{c:139}
effect_on_reporting: No independent journalists were present to document the first two days of the invasion, and the press pool of about 15 reporters that eventually reached Grenada on October 27 remained tightly escorted by the military.{c:138}{c:139}{c:140}

title: Haiti's Duvalier government arrests and deports Radio Haiti-Inter staff, driving its director into exile
issue_of_the_day: Radio Haiti-Inter had built a reputation for independent reporting critical of the Duvalier government at a time when most Haitian media avoided such coverage, drawing sustained official friction toward the station.
outcome_note: Jean Dominique returned to Haiti and to Radio Haiti-Inter in February 1986 after the fall of President-for-life Jean-Claude Duvalier's government.
summary: Under President Jean-Claude Duvalier, Haitian authorities arrested and deported staff of Radio Haiti-Inter, an independent station that had reported critically on the government, forcing its director, journalist Jean Dominique, into exile in 1981. He returned only after Duvalier's government fell in 1986.{c:141}
what_happened: Jean Dominique had worked at Radio Haiti since the late 1960s and bought the station in 1971, renaming it Radio Haiti-Inter and building it into Haiti's leading independent broadcaster under the government of President-for-life Jean-Claude 'Baby Doc' Duvalier, who had succeeded his father, François Duvalier, in 1971. In 1981, authorities arrested and deported Dominique's wife, journalist Michèle Montas, along with other Radio Haiti-Inter staff, and Dominique himself was forced into exile the same year. The station's independent reporting on government abuses had long drawn official friction. Dominique did not return to Haiti until February 1986, after the fall of Duvalier's government ended nearly three decades of rule by father and son. He would later be forced into exile a second time, in 1991, after a separate military takeover, before returning again in 1994.{c:141}{c:142}{c:143}
stated_justification: Haitian authorities did not publish a specific charge against Radio Haiti-Inter's staff; contemporary accounts describe the arrests and deportations as part of the Duvalier government's broader intolerance of the station's independent reporting.{c:141}{c:142}{c:143}
effect_on_reporting: Radio Haiti-Inter lost its director and other staff to arrest, deportation and exile in 1981, suppressing one of Haiti's few independent broadcast voices until Dominique's return five years later.{c:141}{c:142}{c:143}

title: Brazil's Vargas government creates a state messaging department with broad press powers
issue_of_the_day: Vargas had ruled by decree since 1937 under the Estado Novo and used the DIP to promote his government's program and nationalist agenda while suppressing coverage critical of his rule.
outcome_note: The DIP was dissolved in 1945 when the military removed Vargas from power and the Estado Novo dictatorship ended.
summary: President Getúlio Vargas created the Department of Press and state messaging in 1939 during Brazil's Estado Novo dictatorship, giving the government direct control over what newspapers, radio and film could publish. The department operated as a central instrument of press controls for six years, until the Estado Novo ended in 1945.{c:144}{c:145}{c:146}
what_happened: Getúlio Vargas, president of Brazil, had ruled by decree since closing Congress in 1937 and declaring the Estado Novo, or New State. In 1939 his government created the Departamento de Imprensa e Propaganda, the Department of Press and state messaging, known as the DIP, to control news content and promote the government's political program across newspapers, radio and film. The DIP reviewed material before publication, dictated approved themes and language, and could shut down or discipline outlets that stepped outside its guidelines. It functioned as the government's central instrument of press control for six years, shaping coverage of Vargas's policies and suppressing criticism of his government. The DIP was dissolved in 1945 when the Estado Novo ended and Vargas was removed from power by the military, though its intelligence and information functions were later inherited by successor government bodies.{c:144}{c:145}{c:146}
stated_justification: Vargas's government presented the DIP as the coordinating body for national state messaging under the Estado Novo, tasked with promoting the government's program rather than acknowledging a role in suppressing criticism.{c:144}{c:145}{c:146}
effect_on_reporting: Brazilian newspapers, radio stations and filmmakers operated under the DIP's pre-publication review and approved-content guidelines for six years, with the department able to discipline or close outlets that published material outside its guidelines.{c:145}

title: Chile's military government shuts opposition radio stations and newspapers after the 1973 coup
issue_of_the_day: Chile's armed forces were in the process of overthrowing President Salvador Allende's elected government on September 11, 1973, and moved to suppress broadcasters and newspapers that continued to support him as the coup unfolded.
outcome_note: Press restrictions continued under military rule until Chile's return to civilian government in March 1990, after Pinochet lost a 1988 plebiscite on his continued rule.
summary: On the day of the September 11, 1973 military coup that overthrew President Salvador Allende, Chile's armed forces bombed and shut down radio stations that opposed the takeover, arrested journalists and closed newspapers aligned with the ousted government, under the military junta led by Augusto Pinochet.{c:147}{c:148}{c:149}
what_happened: On September 11, 1973, Chile's armed forces, led by General Augusto Pinochet, moved to overthrow the elected government of President Salvador Allende. As the coup unfolded, the military moved against radio stations that continued broadcasting statements opposing the takeover. Radio Magallanes was bombed and hit with gunfire around 10 a.m. and went off the air about 27 minutes later, with four of its journalists arrested in the raid. Radio Candelaria, the last station still opposing the coup, lost its signal shortly before the presidential palace, La Moneda, was bombed at 11:52 a.m. In the following days, the new military government shut down news outlets that had supported Allende's government and barred many journalists identified with them from working in Chile's now military-controlled press, forcing some into what one journalist later called internal exile and driving others abroad.{c:147}{c:148}{c:149}
stated_justification: The military junta that took power on September 11, 1973 treated broadcasters and newspapers that had supported Allende's government as extensions of a political order it had just overthrown, and moved to suppress them as part of securing control.{c:147}{c:148}{c:149}
effect_on_reporting: Radio stations supporting Allende's government went off the air within hours of the coup, journalists were arrested during the takeover, and outlets aligned with the ousted government were shut down and their staff blacklisted from the Chilean press.{c:148}

title: Argentina's military junta threatens journalists with prison for reporting on its opponents
issue_of_the_day: Argentina's military had just overthrown the elected government and moved immediately to prevent reporting sympathetic to leftist groups it had outlawed or reporting it considered damaging to the armed forces' standing.
outcome_note: Argentina returned to civilian, elected government under President Raúl Alfonsín in December 1983, ending the junta's press decrees.
summary: Hours after seizing power on March 24, 1976, Argentina's military junta, led by General Jorge Videla, issued Communiqué No. 19, threatening up to 10 years in prison for reporting favorable to groups it called subversive. Hundreds of journalists were later detained, killed or forced into exile.{c:150}{c:151}{c:152}
what_happened: Argentina's armed forces overthrew President Isabel Perón's government on March 24, 1976 and installed a military junta headed by General Jorge Videla. The same day, the junta issued Communiqué No. 19, threatening imprisonment of up to 10 years for anyone who published or reproduced material from organizations the government had banned, and threatening up to 10 years for reporting that the government said disrupted, harmed or discredited the armed forces. Security forces raided newspapers around the country, arresting and jailing editors and reporters and closing some publications outright. Jacobo Timerman, editor of the newspaper La Opinión, was detained in April 1977 and later held under house arrest. At the English-language Buenos Aires Herald, editor Robert Cox and journalist Andrew Graham-Yooll kept publishing the names of people who had disappeared under the military's rule, until death threats forced both men to leave the country. A subcommittee investigating the period found that roughly 500 journalists had left Argentina for political reasons, while dozens more were reported missing or held in detention centers.{c:150}{c:151}{c:152}
stated_justification: The junta's Communiqué No. 19 framed reporting on groups it had banned, or coverage it considered damaging to the armed forces, as itself a punishable offense carrying years of imprisonment.{c:150}
effect_on_reporting: Newspapers were raided and some closed, editors and reporters were jailed, and rights investigators later documented dozens of journalists missing or in detention and roughly 500 who left the country for political reasons during the military's rule.{c:151}

title: Nazi Germany's Editors Law bars Jewish journalists from the press and puts editors under state direction
issue_of_the_day: Hitler's government, in power only since January 1933, was consolidating control over German public life and moved within months to bring newspapers and their editors directly under state and party direction.
outcome_note: The Editors Law and the Reich Press Chamber ended with Nazi Germany's defeat and unconditional surrender on May 8, 1945.
summary: Nine months after Adolf Hitler became chancellor, Germany's Schriftleitergesetz, or Editors Law, required journalists to register with a new state-controlled Reich Press Chamber and barred non-Aryans from the profession, while directing editors to omit anything judged harmful to the Reich's standing.{c:153}{c:154}{c:155}
what_happened: Adolf Hitler became chancellor of Germany in January 1933, and his government moved quickly to bring the press under state control. On October 4, 1933, it enacted the Schriftleitergesetz, the Editors Law, which required every editor and journalist to register with the newly created Reich Press Chamber, a compulsory professional body under the state messaging Ministry, in order to practice. The Reich Press Chamber kept registries of journalists it certified as racially pure and excluded Jews, and those married to Jews, from the profession entirely. The law's Paragraph 14 required editors to omit from publication anything calculated to weaken the strength of the German state, called the Reich, at home or abroad, and the state messaging Ministry issued daily directives on what could be reported and how. Editors who defied the directives risked losing their registration, dismissal or worse, including imprisonment in a concentration camp.{c:153}{c:154}{c:155}
stated_justification: The law's own text required editors to keep out of print anything judged calculated to weaken the strength of the Reich at home or abroad, casting the requirement as a matter of protecting the German state's standing.{c:154}
effect_on_reporting: Jewish journalists and editors were barred outright from the profession, remaining editors had to follow the state messaging Ministry's daily directives on content, and those who did not risked losing their registration, their jobs or their freedom.{c:155}

title: Soviet Russia creates Glavlit, a central office to review all printed material before publication
issue_of_the_day: The new Soviet government, having just consolidated power after years of revolution and civil war, sought a single, centrally controlled system to replace the uncoordinated military and civilian press controls bodies it had inherited.
outcome_note: Glavlit's authority over publishing was still largely intact through the 1980s, though its standards were relaxed from 1988 under Gorbachev's glasnost policy before its 1991 dissolution.
summary: In 1922, under Vladimir Lenin's government, Soviet Russia created Glavlit, a single agency with final authority to review newspapers, books, plays and even posters before they could be printed or performed. By 1930 no publication in the Soviet Union could appear without its approval.{c:156}{c:157}{c:158}
what_happened: The government led by Vladimir Lenin created Glavlit in 1922 to replace a patchwork of separate military and civilian press controls agencies left over from the Russian Civil War with a single central office. Glavlit, short for the Chief Administration for Literary and Publishing Affairs, held final authority over printed materials and the performing arts, reviewing manuscripts, newspapers and plays before they could reach the public. Its censors watched for material that criticized the Communist Party or the Soviet state, whether directly or by implication, as well as economic or military information judged to threaten state security. By 1930 all printing and publishing in the Soviet Union, down to posters, notepads and theater tickets, required Glavlit's approval before release. The system continued for decades, with its standards loosened only in 1988 under Mikhail Gorbachev's glasnost policy of openness, before Glavlit was dissolved by decree in 1991.{c:156}{c:157}{c:158}
stated_justification: Glavlit's mandate was to prevent the publication of material that could pose a military or economic security threat, or that could be read as critical of the Communist Party or the Soviet state.{c:156}{c:157}{c:158}
effect_on_reporting: No newspaper, book, play or even minor printed item such as a poster or notepad could be published or performed in the Soviet Union without Glavlit's prior approval, a system that lasted essentially unchanged for over six decades.{c:157}

title: Franco's Spain requires state permission to be a journalist under a wartime Press Law
issue_of_the_day: Franco's Nationalist forces were still fighting Spain's civil war in April 1938 and used the new Press Law to consolidate direct control over which newspapers could exist and who could work as a journalist within them.
outcome_note: Spain abolished prior press press controls by decree in April 1977, after Franco's 1975 death, ahead of the 1978 constitution that guaranteed freedom of the press.
summary: While Spain's civil war continued, the Nationalist government led by Francisco Franco enacted a Press Law in April 1938 requiring government permission to found a newspaper, work as a journalist or direct a paper, alongside continued pre-publication press controls and years-long prison terms for vaguely defined offenses.{c:159}{c:160}{c:161}
what_happened: During Spain's civil war, the Nationalist side led by General Francisco Franco enacted a Press Law in April 1938 that placed the country's newspapers under direct state control. The law required government permission to found a newspaper, to work as a professional journalist, or to serve as a newspaper's director, effectively letting the government decide who could practice journalism at all. Pre-publication press controls, already in place since the war's start, continued under the new law. The law also created a vaguely defined offense, the diffusion of false and tendentious news against the authority of the state, that carried prison sentences of three to ten years. The system remained in force, with modifications, for decades; a 1966 law under minister Manuel Fraga presented itself as ending press controls but kept broad limits on content, and between 1966 and 1968 authorities still imposed 180 separate penalties on the press.{c:159}{c:160}{c:161}
stated_justification: The 1938 Press Law and its later penalties applied to what officials called the diffusion of false and tendentious news against the authority of the state, a standard broad enough to cover ordinary critical reporting.{c:160}
effect_on_reporting: Journalists and newspaper directors needed government permission to work at all, coverage remained subject to pre-publication review, and reporters faced years in prison for material officials judged damaging to the state's authority.{c:161}

title: Portugal's Salazar government formally establishes press press controls under a new constitution
issue_of_the_day: Salazar's government was consolidating the Estado Novo behind a new 1933 constitution, and used the moment to formalize a system of press press controls it had for years denied operating.
outcome_note: Portugal's press controls apparatus ended with the Carnation Revolution of April 25, 1974, which overthrew the Estado Novo.
summary: Portugal's government, led by Prime Minister António de Oliveira Salazar, had restricted the press since a 1926 military coup while officially denying it did so. In 1933, alongside a new constitution promising freedom of expression, the government openly established formal press press controls for the first time.{c:162}{c:163}{c:164}
what_happened: After a 1926 military coup, Portugal's governments restricted newspapers while a 1926 decree, known as Law 12008, formally declared that no press controls existed at all. António de Oliveira Salazar, who became prime minister and built the Estado Novo, or New State, brought this contradiction to an end in 1933. That year's new constitution paradoxically guaranteed freedom of expression of thought in any form, even as Salazar's government openly established formal press press controls for the first time, ending the earlier pretense that no such system existed. Newspapers had to submit content for prior review, and the government treated the press as an instrument to be directed rather than a check on official power. Enforcement tightened over the following decade; by 1945 cases against journalists and publishers were being moved to special courts with government-appointed judges, bypassing ordinary judicial oversight.{c:162}{c:163}{c:164}
stated_justification: Portugal's 1933 constitution formally guaranteed freedom of expression of thought in any form whatsoever, even as the same government openly instituted the press press controls it had previously denied running.{c:163}
effect_on_reporting: Newspapers had to submit material for government review before publication, and by 1945 press-related prosecutions could be moved to special courts with judges appointed by the government rather than the ordinary judiciary.{c:164}

title: Soviet-led invasion of Czechoslovakia is followed by the return of government press press controls
issue_of_the_day: Czechoslovakia's Prague Spring reforms, including eased press press controls, had alarmed the Soviet Union and its Warsaw Pact allies, who invaded to reverse the liberalization before it could spread further.
outcome_note: Formal press press controls in Czechoslovakia ended with the Velvet Revolution of November 1989, which brought down Communist Party rule.
summary: Soviet-led Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia on August 20-21, 1968 to end the Prague Spring, a period of liberalization under Alexander Dubček that had included the lifting of press press controls. In the invasion's aftermath, the new leadership reimposed government press controls of the press.{c:165}
what_happened: Czechoslovakia's Communist Party leadership under Alexander Dubček had eased government control of the press during the reform period known as the Prague Spring, which began in January 1968 and let newspapers report and comment with unusual openness for the Eastern Bloc. On the night of August 20 into August 21, 1968, the Soviet Union led Warsaw Pact troops, the alliance of the Soviet Union and its Eastern European allies, into Czechoslovakia to reverse the reforms. Soviet forces occupied radio and television facilities and other key installations as they entered Prague. In the weeks and months that followed, the country's new leadership, under continued Soviet pressure, reestablished government press controls of the press and reimposed controls that had briefly been lifted, part of a broader process Czechoslovaks came to call normalization, which culminated in Dubček's replacement by Gustáv Husák in April 1969.{c:165}{c:166}{c:167}
stated_justification: Soviet and allied leaders described the invasion as necessary to defend socialism in Czechoslovakia against what they called counter-revolutionary tendencies, a framing used to justify reversing the press freedoms of the Prague Spring.{c:165}{c:166}{c:167}
effect_on_reporting: Newspapers, radio and television that had reported with unusual openness during the Prague Spring came back under formal government press controls within weeks of the invasion, ending the brief period of liberalized coverage.{c:166}

title: Poland's martial law government shuts nearly all newspapers and interns journalists overnight
issue_of_the_day: Poland's Solidarity trade union movement had grown into a mass challenge to Communist Party rule through 1980 and 1981, and Jaruzelski's government imposed martial law to suppress the movement and the independent press associated with it.
outcome_note: Martial law was formally lifted on July 22, 1983, though reduced press press controls in Poland continued until the fall of Communist rule in 1989.
summary: On December 13, 1981, General Wojciech Jaruzelski declared martial law in Poland, cutting phone and telex lines, suspending nearly all newspapers, and interning thousands of people, most Solidarity trade union journalists among them, within days.{c:168}{c:169}{c:170}
what_happened: General Wojciech Jaruzelski, Poland's Communist Party leader and prime minister, announced martial law on state television at 6 a.m. on December 13, 1981, saying the country stood at the edge of collapse. The government cut all private telephone and telex lines nationwide and subjected mail to press controls. More than 3,000 people were arrested the first night, a number that reached about 5,000 within a week, and most journalists associated with the independent Solidarity trade union movement were among those detained. Nearly all Polish newspapers were suspended; only the Communist Party's own paper, Trybuna Ludu, and the army daily, Żołnierz Wolności, kept publishing, while television and radio were consolidated into a single channel presented by announcers in military uniform. The Solidarity Press Agency's dispatches to Radio Free Europe, an American-funded broadcaster aimed at Eastern Europe, stopped after that first night.{c:168}{c:169}{c:170}
