title: Minneapolis police projectile permanently blinds photojournalist Linda Tirado
issue_of_the_day: Tirado was documenting the police response to protests over George Floyd's killing in Minneapolis when she was struck; a federal judge later found her case was one of numerous similar reports of journalists being hit by less-lethal munitions during the same unrest.
outcome_note: The city paid $600,000 in a 2022 settlement while continuing to deny that an identified officer fired the projectile.
summary: Freelance photojournalist Linda Tirado was struck in the face by a less-lethal round fired by Minneapolis police while covering protests over George Floyd's killing, permanently blinding her in one eye; the city settled her lawsuit for $600,000 in 2022 while continuing to deny an officer had fired the shot.{c:395}{c:396}{c:397}
what_happened: On May 29, 2020, freelance photojournalist Linda Tirado was covering protests in Minneapolis over George Floyd's killing when she was struck by a tracking round and foam bullets fired by police; one projectile shattered her protective goggles and permanently blinded her in her left eye. Tirado sued the city, police officials and others on June 10, 2020. The Minneapolis Police Department did not respond to requests for comment on the incident. A federal judge, ruling on Tirado's case, found the allegations plausibly suggested a broader pattern, contrary to the First Amendment, of police intentionally using less-lethal munitions against identified journalists, since numerous other reporters described similar experiences during the same unrest. The city reached a $600,000 settlement with Tirado in May 2022, while continuing to deny wrongdoing and never acknowledging that an officer had fired the projectile that blinded her.{c:395}{c:396}{c:397}
stated_justification: The city did not offer a public justification for the specific shot that struck Tirado and denied that any identified officer had fired it.{c:395}{c:396}{c:397}
effect_on_reporting: Tirado said the injury effectively ended a part of her career as a print photojournalist, though she continued working with adapted equipment; the case became a widely cited example of the physical risk journalists faced covering the 2020 protests.{c:395}
unknowns: The identity of the officer who fired the projectile that struck Tirado was never confirmed by the city.

title: FBI raids Project Veritas founder's home over Ashley Biden diary investigation
issue_of_the_day: Project Veritas had obtained and reported on a diary purportedly belonging to Ashley Biden during the 2020 campaign; federal prosecutors were investigating how the diary had been obtained and transported across state lines.
outcome_note: No charges were ever filed against O'Keefe; a court later allowed prosecutors to review the seized phones.
summary: FBI agents raided Project Veritas founder James O'Keefe's New York home and seized his phones as part of an investigation into the alleged theft of a diary belonging to Ashley Biden, President Biden's daughter, which the group had reported on; O'Keefe was never charged.{c:398}{c:399}{c:400}
what_happened: On November 6, 2021, FBI agents searched the Mamaroneck, New York home of Project Veritas founder James O'Keefe and seized two of his iPhones as part of a Justice Department investigation into the alleged theft of a diary belonging to Ashley Biden, daughter of President Biden, which O'Keefe's organization had reported on during the 2020 campaign. O'Keefe said the phones contained reporters' notes, confidential sources unrelated to the diary story and other newsroom material, and said it appeared prosecutors now had journalists "in their sights" for doing their jobs. His attorney said the underlying warrant cited potential charges including misprision of a felony and transporting stolen property across state lines. Two people involved in obtaining the diary pleaded guilty in August 2022; a court later allowed prosecutors to review the seized phones, but no charges were ever filed against O'Keefe himself, and he left Project Veritas in 2023 for unrelated reasons.{c:398}{c:399}{c:400}
stated_justification: The search warrant cited a criminal investigation into the theft and interstate transport of Ashley Biden's diary; prosecutors did not separately justify seizing O'Keefe's phones rather than pursuing other investigative steps.{c:399}
effect_on_reporting: A journalist's personal phones, containing what he said were confidential sources and reporting materials unrelated to the underlying investigation, were seized and later reviewed by federal prosecutors despite no charges ever being filed against him.{c:398}
unknowns: The full contents of what prosecutors reviewed on O'Keefe's phones, and whether any of it was used in other investigations, was not established in the source reviewed.

title: Customs officers seize Grayzone editor's phones at Virginia airport over Iran reporting
issue_of_the_day: Blumenthal had traveled to and reported from Iran, a country CBP's own cited policy treats as grounds for additional scrutiny of travelers who have worked in or visited it.
outcome_note: Customs returned Blumenthal's phones after he sued; litigation continued into discovery over possible data extraction.
summary: U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers stopped Grayzone editor Max Blumenthal at Washington Dulles Airport, questioned him about his reporting trips to Iran, and seized both of his phones without his consent; the phones were returned a week later after he sued.{c:401}
what_happened: On July 10, 2026, U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers stopped Grayzone editor Max Blumenthal at Washington Dulles International Airport, questioned him about his reporting trips to Iran, searched his luggage and seized both of his cellphones without his consent; one officer told him they would "hook them up to machines" to extract the phones' data. CBP said its actions followed standard policy allowing additional scrutiny for travelers who had worked in or visited countries the government designates as state sponsors of terrorism, including Iran. Blumenthal said the stop was obviously connected to his reporting rather than routine screening. He sued on July 16, 2026, and the agency returned his phones the following day; his attorney said the case would proceed to discovery over whether agents had copied data from the devices before returning them.{c:401}{c:402}{c:403}
stated_justification: CBP said "additional scrutiny and increased inspection may be conducted, including if an individual has worked in or traveled to a high-risk country such as a State Sponsor of Terrorism, including Iran."{c:402}
effect_on_reporting: A journalist's phones, containing reporting materials and source contacts, were held by federal border agents for a week, and his attorney said the episode had already discouraged sources from communicating with him and made him wary of further travel.{c:403}
unknowns: Whether CBP extracted or retained data from the phones before returning them was not resolved in the source reviewed.

title: Hungary criminalizes false coronavirus information and grants Orban decree powers
issue_of_the_day: The law was passed as Hungary, like much of Europe, entered its first coronavirus lockdown in March 2020; the government said it needed emergency powers to respond quickly to the pandemic.
outcome_note: Hungary's government said it would end Orban's decree powers by June 20, 2020; the false-information provision's later fate was not established.
summary: Hungary's parliament passed an emergency coronavirus law allowing prison terms of up to five years for spreading information the government deemed false or distorted about the pandemic, and let Prime Minister Viktor Orban rule by decree for an unlimited period.{c:404}
what_happened: On March 30, 2020, Hungary's parliament passed a coronavirus emergency law criminalizing the publication of information the government deemed false or distorted about the pandemic, with penalties of up to five years in prison, and gave Prime Minister Viktor Orban the power to rule by decree for as long as the state of danger lasted, without a fixed end date. Reporters Without Borders said the law could let the government arbitrarily decide which reports were false and use that power against independent newsrooms. The International Press Institute said the law criminalized spreading information deemed to undermine the authorities' pandemic response, with fines and up to five years in prison. Under European pressure, Hungary's government said in late May 2020 it would ask parliament to end the decree powers by June 20, 2020, while the underlying criminal provision on false pandemic information remained on the books in a narrower form.{c:404}{c:405}{c:406}
stated_justification: The government said the emergency powers and the criminal penalty for false pandemic information were necessary to respond quickly and combat what it called disinformation about the coronavirus.{c:404}{c:405}{c:406}
effect_on_reporting: Hungarian outlets faced the prospect of prison sentences for coronavirus reporting the government might later deem false or distorted, at the same time the government could rule by decree without a parliamentary check.{c:405}
unknowns: Whether the criminal penalty for false pandemic information was narrowed or repealed after the state of danger ended was not established in the sources reviewed.

title: Myanmar junta revokes five outlets' licenses and raids newsrooms after coup
issue_of_the_day: The outlets had been covering nationwide protests against the military's February 1, 2021 seizure of power from Myanmar's elected government, coverage the junta sought to stop by removing the outlets' legal authorization to operate.
outcome_note: The five outlets' licenses were not restored; CPJ counted at least 32 journalists still imprisoned as of July 2021.
summary: Weeks after seizing power, Myanmar's military junta revoked the operating licenses of five independent media outlets covering protests against the coup and raided two of their newsrooms, seizing computers and files; journalists from the outlets were later arrested and charged under a broadened penal-code provision on spreading 'false news.'{c:407}
what_happened: On March 8 and 9, 2021, Myanmar's military junta revoked the licenses of five independent outlets, Mizzima, Myanmar Now, 7Day News, Democratic Voice of Burma and Khit Thit Media, which had been covering protests against the February 1 coup. Soldiers and police raided Myanmar Now's Yangon office, seizing computers, documents and server equipment, and raided Mizzima's head office the following day. Two weeks after the coup, the junta had broadened Article 505(a) of the penal code to criminalize spreading what it called false news, raising the maximum penalty from two to three years in prison; journalists from the affected outlets were later arrested and charged under the provision while covering the protests. The Committee to Protect Journalists said the junta must immediately reverse the license suspensions and let the outlets resume normal operations.{c:407}{c:408}{c:409}
stated_justification: Myanmar's Ministry of Information did not respond to CPJ's request for comment explaining the license revocations; the junta separately said in public statements that it respected media freedom while warning outlets against using words like "coup" and "junta."{c:407}{c:408}{c:409}
effect_on_reporting: Five of Myanmar's most prominent independent outlets lost their legal authority to operate inside the country, and reporting on the coup and its aftermath increasingly had to be produced from exile or underground.{c:408}

title: Belarus blocks Tut.by and arrests its editors as 'extremist'
issue_of_the_day: Tut.by had continued reporting on the government's response to protests following the disputed August 2020 presidential election that kept Alexander Lukashenko in power; authorities revoked the outlet's official media registration in January 2021.
outcome_note: Tut.by remained blocked and its former staff continued reporting from exile as Zerkalo; the criminal proceedings against staff continued.
summary: Belarusian authorities blocked access to Tut.by, the country's most-read independent news site, searched its offices in three cities and arrested at least eleven staff, including its editor-in-chief, citing alleged media-law violations after the site had already lost its official media status.{c:410}{c:411}{c:412}{c:413}
what_happened: On May 19, 2021, Belarusian authorities blocked online access to Tut.by, the country's most-visited independent news site, and searched its headquarters in Minsk and regional offices in Brest and Hrodna, arresting at least eleven employees, including editor-in-chief Marina Zolotova and publisher Volha Loyka, and opening criminal proceedings against the outlet's leadership. The information ministry said the site had committed "multiple media law violations, including the publication of banned information." Reporters Without Borders said the accusations were invented as a pretext to shut down one of the country's most popular outlets, which had already lost its official media status in January 2021 and whose staff separately faced tax-fraud charges RSF called fabricated. The outlet later continued reporting from exile under the name Zerkalo.{c:410}{c:411}{c:412}{c:413}
stated_justification: Belarus's information ministry said it was acting against "multiple media law violations, including the publication of banned information," and Deputy Information Minister Andrey Kuncevic said the government would continue "protecting the country's information space."{c:410}
effect_on_reporting: Belarus's largest independent news site was blocked inside the country and its editorial leadership arrested, forcing its journalists to continue reporting from exile under a new name.{c:411}{c:413}

title: Russia criminalizes 'fake' reporting on the military, up to 15 years in prison
issue_of_the_day: The law followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, and was aimed at reporting on the war that differed from the Russian defense ministry's official statements about casualties and military conduct.
outcome_note: The law remained in force; independent outlets that avoided closure continued operating from outside Russia.
summary: Russia's parliament passed a law criminalizing the publication of information about the military that contradicts official statements, with penalties up to 15 years in prison, prompting Novaya Gazeta to pull its Ukraine war coverage and the BBC, CNN and other outlets to suspend operations inside Russia.{c:414}{c:415}{c:416}{c:417}
what_happened: On March 4, 2022, Russia's parliament passed a law criminalizing the publication of what officials called deliberately false information about the military, including reporting on the invasion of Ukraine that contradicted official statements, with penalties of up to three years for a basic offense and up to 15 years in cases deemed to have caused severe consequences. Parliament speaker Vyacheslav Volodin said the law was meant to protect Russian soldiers and the truth. Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia's few remaining independent outlets, removed its Ukraine war coverage from its site, warning that restrictions on reporting had moved from threats of blocking outlets to threats of criminal prosecution of journalists and ordinary citizens. The BBC suspended its Russian news operations, with director-general Tim Davie saying the safety of staff came first, and other foreign broadcasters and independent Russian outlets closed or left the country in the days that followed.{c:414}{c:415}{c:416}{c:417}
stated_justification: Parliament speaker Vyacheslav Volodin said the law was needed "to protect our soldiers and officers, and to protect the truth."{c:414}
effect_on_reporting: Independent and foreign reporting on the war from inside Russia largely ended within days, as outlets weighed the risk of years-long prison sentences for staff against continuing to report on the invasion.{c:415}{c:417}

title: Indian tax authorities search BBC offices weeks after Modi documentary ban
issue_of_the_day: The searches followed the government's ban, weeks earlier, of the BBC documentary 'India: The Modi Question,' which examined Modi's record as Gujarat's chief minister during 2002 riots that killed mostly Muslims.
outcome_note: No penalty or further tax action against the BBC was reported; the broadcaster's India operations continued.
summary: India's Income Tax Department searched BBC offices in Delhi and Mumbai for alleged tax evasion, three weeks after the government used emergency powers to block a BBC documentary examining Prime Minister Narendra Modi's response to 2002 communal violence.{c:418}{c:419}{c:420}
what_happened: On February 14, 2023, India's Income Tax Department conducted what officials called surveys, sealing off and searching BBC offices in Delhi and Mumbai and confiscating documents and journalists' phones, in what the government said was an investigation into tax evasion. The searches came about three weeks after the government invoked emergency powers under India's Information Technology Rules to block domestic access to the BBC's two-part documentary 'India: The Modi Question,' which examined Modi's response to 2002 communal violence in Gujarat, where he was then chief minister. A spokesperson for the governing party called the BBC "the most corrupt organization in the world," while Human Rights Watch said the raid and the documentary ban were part of an escalating pattern of using government agencies to pressure civil-society groups and media outlets. India's Editors Guild called the searches a continuation of a trend of using government agencies to pressure press organizations.{c:418}{c:419}{c:420}
stated_justification: Officials said the tax searches were routine "surveys, not searches," aimed at investigating alleged tax evasion by the BBC.{c:418}
effect_on_reporting: The BBC's Indian bureaus lost access to documents and staff phones for the length of the search, coming so soon after the documentary ban that press-freedom groups treated the two actions as connected pressure on the same outlet.{c:419}
unknowns: The outcome of the tax investigation itself was not established in the source reviewed.

title: Bombay High Court strikes down India's government 'fact check unit' rule
issue_of_the_day: The government said the Fact Check Unit was needed to combat misinformation about its own policies and announcements online, at a time when it separately faced criticism over content restrictions ahead of India's 2024 general election.
outcome_note: The Bombay High Court struck down the rule, finding its key terms 'vague and overbroad,' after the Supreme Court had already stayed its operation.
summary: India's 2023 amendment to its Information Technology Rules empowered a government-run Fact Check Unit to label online content about the central government 'fake' or 'false' and require its removal; comedian Kunal Kamra and media groups challenged it, and the Bombay High Court struck the rule down as unconstitutionally vague.{c:421}{c:422}{c:423}
what_happened: In 2023, India's government amended its Information Technology Rules to create a Fact Check Unit empowered to identify online content about the central government's own affairs as "fake, false or misleading" and require platforms to remove it or lose their legal protection from liability for user content. Comedian Kunal Kamra, the Editors Guild of India and the Association of Indian Magazines challenged the rule, arguing there was no constitutional "right to the truth" that could justify a government body policing facts about itself. India's Supreme Court stayed the unit's operation while the case proceeded. After a split verdict, a tie-breaking judge on the Bombay High Court struck down the rule in September 2024, finding its key terms "vague and overbroad" and the government's own definition of misinformation legally unsound.{c:421}{c:422}{c:423}
stated_justification: The government said the Fact Check Unit was needed to address "misinformation concerning the Central Government's affairs" and to identify content that was "fake" or "false."{c:421}
effect_on_reporting: Had it taken effect, the rule would have let a government body decide which online statements about its own policies counted as false and require platforms to remove them, a power that never came into force because of the legal challenge.{c:422}

title: Guatemala convicts investigative journalist Jose Ruben Zamora on money-laundering charge
issue_of_the_day: El Periodico had published more than 120 investigations into government corruption since January 2020 before its forced closure in May 2023, shortly before Zamora's conviction.
outcome_note: Zamora's case continued through appeals and changing custody arrangements; he remained in the criminal justice system.
summary: A Guatemalan court convicted El Periodico founder Jose Ruben Zamora of money laundering and sentenced him to six years in prison, months after his newspaper, known for investigating government corruption, was forced to close; press-freedom groups said the case was connected to his investigative reporting rather than the financial charge alone.{c:424}
what_happened: On June 14, 2023, a Guatemalan court convicted journalist Jose Ruben Zamora, founder of the investigative newspaper El Periodico, of laundering approximately $40,000, sentencing him to six years in prison and a fine of more than $38,000. Zamora had been arrested the previous July, and El Periodico, which had published more than 120 investigations into government corruption since January 2020, was forced to close in May 2023, with its leadership citing pressure on its advertisers and on its operations. Zamora said prosecutors had "treated us like criminals" and destroyed evidence; his son said the state had effectively kidnapped an innocent man. The Committee to Protect Journalists said the case sent a message that reporting on corruption could itself be treated as a crime, and the court separately found that Zamora's reporting had harmed the Guatemalan economy.{c:424}{c:425}{c:426}{c:427}
stated_justification: The court convicted Zamora of money laundering and found that his conduct had harmed the Guatemalan economy; President Giammattei's government said Guatemala had a free press and denied any political motivation.{c:424}{c:425}{c:426}{c:427}
effect_on_reporting: One of Guatemala's most prominent investigative outlets closed and its founder was imprisoned within the same year, a sequence press-freedom groups said sent a message to other Guatemalan journalists covering official corruption.{c:425}{c:427}

title: Nicaragua strips 94 political opponents, including journalists, of citizenship
issue_of_the_day: The rulings followed years of pressure on Nicaragua's independent press, including the earlier forced closure of the country's oldest newspaper, La Prensa, and came days after Ortega's government released 222 jailed dissidents to the United States and stripped their citizenship as well.
outcome_note: Citizenship was not restored to those named; Ortega's government continued comparable actions against critics afterward.
summary: A Nicaraguan appeals court stripped 94 government opponents, including exiled journalists Carlos Fernando Chamorro and Alvaro Navarro, of their citizenship, days after President Daniel Ortega released 222 political prisoners to the United States and immediately declared them stateless too.{c:428}{c:429}{c:430}
what_happened: On February 16, 2023, a Nicaraguan appeals court stripped 94 government opponents, described in the ruling as human rights defenders, politicians, journalists and students, of their Nicaraguan citizenship, on top of 222 political prisoners flown to the United States days earlier who had already been declared stateless. Journalists Carlos Fernando Chamorro and Alvaro Navarro were among those named. Appeals Court Justice Ernesto Rodriguez Mejia said those affected were guilty of "spreading false news" and conspiring to undermine national integrity. Navarro responded that he remained Nicaraguan regardless of the ruling. Civil Rights Defenders said Ortega was clearly trying to eliminate anyone who stood up against his government and called for international bodies to raise Nicaragua's deteriorating human rights record.{c:428}{c:429}{c:430}
stated_justification: The court found those whose citizenship had been revoked guilty of "spreading false news" and "conspiracy to undermine national integrity."{c:428}
effect_on_reporting: Exiled Nicaraguan journalists, already unable to work safely inside the country, lost their legal nationality entirely, cutting off their ability to hold a Nicaraguan passport or return under any legal status.{c:429}

title: Slovakia's parliament dissolves public broadcaster RTVS, replaces it with STVR
issue_of_the_day: Fico's government accused RTVS of one-sided, activist coverage against it, a complaint it made after RTVS reporting the government considered unfavorable during Fico's return to power in late 2023.
outcome_note: STVR replaced RTVS as planned; the ousted director-general kept only his separate parliamentary mandate.
summary: Slovakia's parliament, controlled by Prime Minister Robert Fico's coalition, dissolved public broadcaster RTVS and replaced it with a new entity, STVR, whose director is now chosen through a process giving parliament and the culture ministry more direct control, prompting protests and criticism from the European Union.{c:431}{c:432}{c:433}
what_happened: Slovakia's parliament passed a law dissolving the public broadcaster RTVS and creating a successor, Slovak Television and Radio (STVR), which took effect on July 4, 2024. Under the new structure, parliament and the culture ministry nominate nine council members who select STVR's director-general, replacing RTVS's previous, more independent selection process; the displaced RTVS director, Lubos Machaj, kept only his separate parliamentary mandate through 2027. The parliamentary culture committee's chairman defended the change, describing RTVS as an "activist TV" whose editors lacked political neutrality. Opposition lawmaker Zora Jaurova said private media owners were being pressured to accept a different approach to political coverage, and Slovak journalist Ivan Brada said the country appeared to be following Hungary's path toward government-controlled media. Thousands protested in Bratislava, and European institutions criticized the law.{c:431}{c:432}{c:433}
stated_justification: The parliamentary committee chairman overseeing the bill said RTVS operated as an "activist TV" whose editorial staff lacked political neutrality.{c:431}
effect_on_reporting: Slovakia's public broadcaster was dissolved and re-formed under a leadership-selection process giving the governing coalition direct influence over who runs it, a structural change press-freedom monitors said increased the government's leverage over public-service journalism.{c:432}

title: Georgia enacts 'foreign influence' law requiring media to register as foreign-backed
issue_of_the_day: The governing Georgian Dream party framed the law as protecting Georgian sovereignty against foreign-funded groups it accused of trying to organize unrest, at a time when the party also faced growing opposition ahead of Georgia's 2024 parliamentary election.
outcome_note: The law took effect despite mass protests and international criticism; the governing party did not withdraw it.
summary: Georgia's parliament passed a law requiring media and civil-society groups that receive 20 percent or more of their funding from abroad to register as organizations "serving the interests of a foreign power," over mass street protests and international criticism that the label would be used to marginalize independent outlets.{c:434}{c:435}{c:436}
what_happened: Georgia's parliament passed the "law on transparency of foreign influence" in May 2024, requiring media outlets and non-governmental organizations that receive twenty percent or more of their annual revenue from foreign sources to register with the justice ministry as "organizations serving the interests of a foreign power," subjecting them to additional reporting requirements, inspections and fines of roughly $9,300 for noncompliance. Human Rights Watch's Europe director, Hugh Williamson, said labeling independent groups and media as serving foreign interests was intended to marginalize and stifle critical voices, and called on Georgian authorities to drop the bill. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze defended the law as directed at groups he said were trying to "organize a revolution," promote what he called "LGBT propaganda," and "discredit the police, judiciary, and the Georgian Orthodox Church." Mass protests in Tbilisi and statements from United Nations experts condemning the law did not stop its passage.{c:434}{c:435}{c:436}
stated_justification: Prime Minister Kobakhidze said the law addressed groups attempting to "organize a revolution" and to "discredit the police, judiciary, and the Georgian Orthodox Church."{c:435}
effect_on_reporting: Independent Georgian outlets that rely on foreign grants faced a stigmatizing official label, new inspections and fines, pressure press-freedom groups said was designed to make continued foreign-funded reporting more difficult.{c:434}

title: Hong Kong court convicts Stand News editors of sedition
issue_of_the_day: The prosecution centered on opinion pieces and interviews Stand News had published examining Hong Kong's 2019 protests and the 2020 National Security Law, coverage prosecutors said smeared the security law and law enforcement.
outcome_note: Both editors were sentenced in September 2024; no reversal of the convictions was reported.
summary: A Hong Kong court convicted former Stand News editors Chung Pui-kuen and Patrick Lam of conspiring to publish seditious material, under a colonial-era law, over articles the outlet had run before police raided its newsroom and it closed at the end of 2021.{c:437}
what_happened: On August 29, 2024, Hong Kong District Court Judge Kwok Wai-kin convicted former Stand News editor-in-chief Chung Pui-kuen and acting editor-in-chief Patrick Lam of conspiring to publish and reproduce seditious material, finding that 11 of 17 articles the prosecution presented had been seditious under a sedition law dating to the colonial era. Stand News had already ceased operating in December 2021 after a police raid on its offices. Chung argued in response that free speech should not be limited to eliminating dangerous ideas but should instead be used to counter them. A U.S. State Department spokesperson said the verdict directly harmed media freedom. Both editors were sentenced on September 26, 2024, facing up to two years in prison.{c:437}{c:438}{c:439}{c:440}
stated_justification: The court found that the articles were seditious because they were capable of undermining public confidence in the Hong Kong or Chinese central government, and prosecutors argued certain pieces promoted ideologies the law prohibited or smeared the security law and police.{c:437}{c:438}{c:439}{c:440}
effect_on_reporting: A once-prominent Hong Kong outlet had already closed under police pressure, and the criminal conviction of its editors for material it had published established that ordinary opinion journalism about the security law could carry a prison sentence.{c:438}

title: Milei's government shuts down Argentina's state news agency Telam
issue_of_the_day: Milei had campaigned against what he called wasteful and politically one-sided state spending, and Telam, founded in 1945, had long been associated with the governments of the Kirchner political movement he defeated in the 2023 election.
outcome_note: Telam's original newsroom remained closed; the agency was later reorganized as a smaller state communications operation.
summary: President Javier Milei's government fenced off and shut down Telam, Argentina's state-owned news agency, calling it a public-relations operation for the prior Kirchnerist governments; unions and journalist groups called the closure one of the most serious blows to press freedom in decades of Argentine democracy.{c:441}
what_happened: On the night of March 3 into March 4, 2024, Milei's government fenced off Telam's Buenos Aires offices and blocked staff from entering, taking the agency's website offline and placing its roughly seven hundred employees on seven days of paid leave while the closure proceeded. Milei said it was wrong for a poor country's government to spend public money buying journalists' favor, calling Telam "a covert propaganda ministry" and "a Kirchnerist propaganda agency for the last decades." The Buenos Aires Press Union, SiPreBA, called the closure one of the worst actions against freedom of expression in forty years of Argentine democracy, and the Argentine Journalism Forum, Fopea, said the decision would deepen intolerance toward journalism. Workers and press-freedom advocates organized protests, including a symbolic gathering around the building, but the closure proceeded.{c:441}{c:442}{c:443}{c:444}
stated_justification: Milei said it was "immoral that in a poor country like ours, the government spends the people's money to buy the will of journalists," describing Telam as "a covert propaganda ministry."{c:442}
effect_on_reporting: Argentina's national wire service, which many regional and local outlets relied on for national and international news feeds, stopped operating, and roughly seven hundred journalists and staff lost their positions.{c:443}

title: Serbian police strike, detain and disarm journalists covering anti-government protests
issue_of_the_day: The protests, which grew through the summer of 2025, followed months of demonstrations against President Aleksandar Vucic's government that began after a deadly railway-station canopy collapse in Novi Sad in late 2024.
outcome_note: The interior ministry did not respond to CPJ's request for comment, and no officer was reported disciplined for the incidents documented.
summary: The Committee to Protect Journalists documented at least 28 Serbian journalists reporting being struck, detained, sprayed with chemical irritants or having their equipment destroyed by police between June and September 2025 while covering nationwide anti-government protests; the interior ministry did not respond to CPJ's request for comment.{c:445}
what_happened: Between June and September 2025, Serbian police repeatedly used force against journalists covering nationwide anti-government protests, according to a Committee to Protect Journalists report published September 25, 2025 documenting at least 28 affected journalists. On September 5 in Novi Sad, police kicked reporter Emir Kahrimanovic despite his visible press vest, forced Vreme reporter Katarina Stevanovic to lie on the ground for about fifteen minutes, and grabbed and smashed KTV reporter Nemanja Sarovic's microphone while he was reporting live. On September 1, an officer seized Beta news agency reporter Bozidar Milovac's phone and forced him to delete footage despite his identifying himself as a journalist. In earlier incidents in Belgrade and other cities in July and August, reporters described being struck with batons and shields, sprayed with an unknown chemical substance, and having memory cards destroyed. CPJ's Europe representative called for swift, transparent investigations and accountability for the officers involved; the interior ministry did not respond to CPJ's request for comment.{c:445}{c:446}{c:447}
stated_justification: No Serbian official offered a public justification for the specific incidents documented; the interior ministry did not respond to CPJ's request for comment.{c:445}{c:446}{c:447}
effect_on_reporting: Journalists covering the protests described routinely facing physical force, confiscation or destruction of equipment, and orders to stop filming, even when visibly identified as press, narrowing on-the-ground coverage of the demonstrations.{c:447}
unknowns: Whether any internal investigation into individual officers' conduct was opened was not established in the source reviewed.

title: Ethiopia arrests at least six journalists including Sheger FM staff over election-year coverage
issue_of_the_day: The arrests came ahead of Ethiopia's national elections scheduled for 2026, after the Ethiopian Media Authority ordered Sheger FM to remove an August 29, 2025 broadcast it said was one-sided and incited violence.
outcome_note: Some journalists were granted bail while an appeal proceeded; the media authority's order against Sheger FM remained in force.
summary: Ethiopian authorities arrested at least six journalists between August and September 2025, including three from Sheger FM after the Ethiopian Media Authority ordered the station to delete a broadcast it accused of bias and inciting violence, ahead of national elections scheduled for 2026.{c:448}{c:449}{c:450}
what_happened: Between August and September 2025, Ethiopian authorities arrested at least six journalists and media workers, including radio host Khadar Mohamed Ismail on August 5, radio host Abdulsemed Mohammed on August 11, and journalist Yonas Amare, who was abducted on August 13 and released on August 22 along with Mohammed. On September 3, Sheger FM journalists Tigist Zerihun, Mintamir Tsegaw and Eshete Assefa were arrested after the Ethiopian Media Authority ordered the station to delete an August 29 broadcast it accused of bias and inciting violence. Human Rights Watch said the authorities' renewed efforts to limit independent reporting were aimed at preventing public scrutiny of the government ahead of elections scheduled for 2026, adding that a free press mattered more, not less, in the run-up to a vote. Some of the Sheger FM journalists were granted bail in mid-September while an appeal proceeded.{c:448}{c:449}{c:450}
stated_justification: The Ethiopian Media Authority accused the Sheger FM broadcast of "bias and inciting violence" when it ordered the station to remove it.{c:448}
effect_on_reporting: Independent Ethiopian broadcasters described feeling pressure to delete their own content and hold back coverage under threat of arrest, narrowing reporting on politically sensitive events ahead of the 2026 election.{c:449}
unknowns: The final legal outcome for each of the six journalists named was not established in the source reviewed.

title: Pakistan amends cybercrime law to create new agency policing 'fake' online content
issue_of_the_day: The government said the amendment was needed to curb online disinformation, but journalists said the new offense's vague wording, covering content merely believed likely to cause "fear, panic, disorder or unrest," gave authorities broad discretion over ordinary reporting.
outcome_note: The amendment remained law despite nationwide journalist protests and a Human Rights Watch call for its repeal.
summary: Pakistan's parliament amended the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act to create a new Social Media Protection and Regulatory Authority with power to block online content and a Social Media Protection Tribunal, and made spreading information deemed 'fake or false' punishable by up to three years in prison, prompting nationwide journalist protests.{c:451}{c:452}{c:453}{c:454}
what_happened: On January 29, 2025, Pakistan's parliament passed amendments to the 2016 Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act creating a government-appointed Social Media Protection and Regulatory Authority, empowered to order the removal or blocking of online content, and a separate Social Media Protection Tribunal to hear related cases. A new provision, Section 26A, made it a crime punishable by up to three years in prison or a fine of about $7,000 to knowingly disseminate information believed to be false or fake and likely to cause "fear, panic, disorder or unrest." The Pakistan Press Foundation said the lack of clarity around the amendments raised questions about the government's real intent, and Human Rights Watch called for the law's repeal, saying it lacked any exemption protecting journalistic work. The Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists organized nationwide protests, calling the law an infringement on people's rights.{c:451}{c:452}{c:453}{c:454}
stated_justification: The law's Section 26A targets the "intentional dissemination, exhibition or transmission of information...that the sender knows or believes to be false or fake and likely to cause or create a sense of public fear, panic, disorder or unrest."{c:452}
effect_on_reporting: Journalists faced a vaguely worded criminal offense, enforced by a government-appointed authority and tribunal rather than the courts, for publishing information officials could later deem false, with no exemption for journalistic work.{c:451}{c:454}

title: Journalists beaten in Bangladesh in separate incidents as interim government drafts new cyber laws
issue_of_the_day: The incidents occurred six months into the interim government that took power after Sheikh Hasina's government fell in August 2024, a period in which press-freedom groups said journalists faced both continued street violence and new draft cyber-security legislation.
outcome_note: No arrests were reported in the incidents described, and the proposed cyber ordinances remained under review.
summary: On a single day in February 2025, groups of men beat at least eight journalists in two separate incidents in rural Bangladesh while they investigated a medical-negligence tip and a land dispute; the incidents came as the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus drafted new cyber ordinances rights groups said could add legal risk on top of the physical one.{c:455}
what_happened: On February 3, 2025, ten to twelve men beat Samakal correspondent Shohag Khan Sujon with a hammer and knife while he investigated allegations of medical negligence in Shariatpur district, and four other journalists who intervened were also beaten. The same day, in Laxmipur district, four correspondents covering a land dispute were beaten with bamboo sticks by a separate group that also fired guns, wounding one journalist with shrapnel. Days earlier, British freelance journalist Shafiur Rahman received threatening emails after publishing an article about a government security meeting, warning him to "stop or suffer the consequences." The Committee to Protect Journalists said the interim government's draft Cyber Protection Ordinance and Personal Data Protection Ordinance, introduced in January 2025, risked giving authorities broad new power over online content and user data on top of the continuing physical violence journalists faced covering local disputes.{c:455}{c:456}{c:457}
stated_justification: No government official offered a public justification for the beatings, which were carried out by private individuals; the interim government described its draft cyber ordinances as necessary data-protection and security measures.{c:455}{c:456}{c:457}
effect_on_reporting: Reporters covering local corruption and land disputes in rural Bangladesh faced serious physical violence in a single day, while a freelance journalist covering national-security matters received written threats, illustrating the range of pressure facing the press during the political transition.{c:456}

title: Venezuela detains, expels and restricts journalists after disputed 2024 election
issue_of_the_day: Venezuela's July 28, 2024 election, in which the National Electoral Council declared Maduro the winner without releasing detailed vote tallies opposition figures disputed, triggered protests and a surge of restrictions on the journalists covering them.
outcome_note: Detained journalists faced continuing prosecution, and social-platform restrictions remained in place after the documented period.
summary: In the two weeks after Venezuela's disputed July 28, 2024 presidential election, Reporters Without Borders documented 70 press-freedom violations, including nine detentions, nine expulsions of foreign correspondents and the suspension of the social media platform X, as President Nicolas Maduro's government moved to control coverage of the disputed result.{c:458}
what_happened: In the fifteen days after Venezuela's July 28, 2024 election, Reporters Without Borders documented 70 press-freedom violations, including 18 access restrictions, 30 cases of threats or coercion, nine detentions, nine expulsions of foreign journalists and four instances of physical violence. Colombian journalists Carolina Trinidad and Vanessa de la Torre were expelled from the Caracas airport without explanation on election day, Chilean journalists Ivan Nunez and Jose Luis Tapia were held incommunicado at a military post until their embassy intervened, and Spanish journalist Alvaro Nieto was deported after a two-hour interrogation. Venezuelan photojournalists and broadcasters, including Yousnel Alvarado and Deisy Pena, were detained and, in some cases, held on terrorism-related charges. The government also opened a criminal investigation into the opposition-aligned results website ResultadosConVzla, suspended X for ten days and blocked Signal and Reddit. RSF's Latin America director said the pattern of violations showed the government's determination to limit public debate.{c:458}{c:459}{c:460}
stated_justification: No specific public justification for the individual detentions and expulsions was documented; the government separately described the platform suspensions as necessary to prevent the spread of what it called disinformation about the election.{c:458}{c:459}{c:460}
effect_on_reporting: Foreign correspondents were expelled or detained within days of the vote, Venezuelan journalists were jailed on serious charges including terrorism, and major communication platforms were blocked or suspended, sharply narrowing independent coverage of the disputed result.{c:459}

title: Turkish authorities detain three journalists under 'disinformation' law
issue_of_the_day: Sardan had written about an alleged Turkish intelligence report on judicial corruption, which the government's Center for Combating Disinformation denied existed; Halk TV's Dincer Gokce had reported on people released from prison who were later linked to further crimes.
outcome_note: Two of the three journalists were released within a day; Tolga Sardan remained jailed pending trial.
summary: Turkish authorities detained three journalists, jailing columnist Tolga Sardan pending trial, under a 2022 law criminalizing the spread of disinformation, after the government's own disinformation-fighting body disputed their reporting on a leaked intelligence document and a story about released prisoners.{c:461}
what_happened: On November 1 and 2, 2023, Turkish authorities detained T24 columnist Tolga Sardan, Halk TV news editor Dincer Gokce and Kisa Dalga reporter Cengiz Erdinc under Turkiye's 2022 law criminalizing the spread of what officials call disinformation. Sardan was jailed pending trial after writing about an intelligence report on judicial corruption that the government's Center for Combating Disinformation said did not exist. Gokce was released after a court ordered him to read books about journalism, over an article about people released from prison who authorities said had been wrongly described. Erdinc was released the following day. The Committee to Protect Journalists called on Turkish authorities to release Sardan and Erdinc without delay and said the vague law would continue to stifle reporting in the country.{c:461}{c:462}{c:463}
stated_justification: Turkey's Center for Combating Disinformation denied the existence of the intelligence report Sardan had written about, and authorities said Gokce's article about released prisoners had proven inaccurate.{c:461}{c:462}{c:463}
effect_on_reporting: A columnist was jailed pending trial and another journalist was ordered by a court to read books about journalism, over stories the government's own disinformation body disputed rather than a court finding of falsity through an ordinary defamation process.{c:462}

title: Tunisia's cybercrime decree pushes jailed-journalist count to highest since 1992
issue_of_the_day: Decree-Law 54, issued by President Kais Saied in 2022 without a sitting parliament, criminalized spreading what authorities deem "false news" online, and by January 2025 had become the basis for jailing a record number of Tunisian journalists.
outcome_note: Decree-Law 54 remained in force and continued to produce new prosecutions, which CPJ said brought jailed-journalist numbers to a record.
summary: The Committee to Protect Journalists found at least four journalists imprisoned under Tunisia's 2022 Decree-Law 54 on cybercrime as of January 2025, including radio hosts Mourad Zghidi and Borhen Bsaies, pushing the country's jailed-journalist count to its highest since 1992 under President Kais Saied.{c:464}
what_happened: The Committee to Protect Journalists reported on January 16, 2025 that at least four of five imprisoned Tunisian journalists were convicted under Decree-Law 54, a 2022 cybercrime decree President Kais Saied issued while ruling by decree without a sitting parliament. Radio hosts Mourad Zghidi and Borhen Bsaies of IFM each received one-year sentences, commentator Sonia Dahmani's one-year sentence was reduced to eight months on appeal before she received an additional two-year sentence, and journalist Mohamed Boughaleb received six months on a separate defamation charge. The head of Tunisia's journalists' union, Ziad Debbar, said the decree had turned every journalist into a suspect. The International Commission of Jurists said Tunisian authorities were using the decree to arbitrarily restrict dissenting voices, in violation of the country's human rights obligations, subjecting journalists, politicians and rights defenders to prosecution, investigation and imprisonment.{c:464}{c:465}{c:466}
stated_justification: Decree-Law 54 targets content that "produces, spreads, disseminates, sends or writes false news" seen as threatening "rights of others, public safety or national defense or sowing terror."{c:465}
effect_on_reporting: Tunisia, once cited as a rare post-Arab Spring press-freedom success, reached its highest count of imprisoned journalists since 1992, with radio hosts and commentators serving sentences of six months to more than two years for broadcast commentary and online statements.{c:464}{c:465}{c:466}

title: Tanzania shuts down internet access on election day amid unrest
issue_of_the_day: The shutdown coincided with a disputed general election and protests against President Samia Suluhu Hassan's government, which Human Rights Watch later said was followed by killings and broader restrictions once the results were announced.
outcome_note: Authorities did not explain the shutdown, and disruptions to social platforms continued for several days after the vote.
summary: Tanzania's government restricted internet and social-media access on October 29, 2025, as citizens voted in a general election marked by protests, cutting national internet traffic by nearly 90 percent and leaving both local and foreign journalists unable to report on the vote and its aftermath in real time.{c:467}
what_happened: On October 29, 2025, as Tanzanians voted in a general election, national internet traffic began falling sharply around 12:30 p.m. local time, dropping to nearly 90 percent below the previous week's levels, according to monitoring cited by TechCabal; three journalists in Dar es Salaam and Arusha said social media platforms were unreachable without a virtual private network. Neither the Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority nor telecom operators responded publicly to questions about the outage, and Tanzanian authorities did not issue a statement explaining it. Human Rights Watch reported on November 4, 2025 that the shutdown prevented media from reporting on the election and the protests that followed, and said authorities appeared to have also blocked foreign journalists from covering the vote by not responding to their accreditation applications.{c:467}{c:468}{c:469}{c:470}
stated_justification: Tanzanian authorities did not issue a public statement explaining the internet restrictions.{c:467}{c:468}{c:469}{c:470}
effect_on_reporting: Local and international journalists lost the ability to report in real time on the election and the protests that followed, while some foreign correspondents said their accreditation requests to cover the vote went unanswered.{c:469}{c:470}
unknowns: The precise date full connectivity was restored was not established in the sources reviewed.

title: Court orders RCMP to stop restricting press access at Fairy Creek logging blockades
issue_of_the_day: The RCMP was enforcing a court injunction won by logging company Teal-Jones against protesters blocking old-growth logging roads near Fairy Creek on Vancouver Island, and had required journalists to check in and stay escorted rather than observe enforcement directly.
outcome_note: The court granted the media coalition's request, requiring the RCMP to account for press access in future enforcement decisions.
summary: A British Columbia court found the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had failed to justify wide exclusion zones that kept journalists away from its enforcement of a logging injunction at the Fairy Creek old-growth blockades, and ordered police to keep the media's role in a free society in mind when deciding whether to remove or arrest reporters.{c:471}
what_happened: Through the summer of 2021, journalists covering the RCMP's enforcement of a court injunction against old-growth logging protesters at Fairy Creek, on Vancouver Island in British Columbia, said police required them to check in at set times and remain escorted rather than observe arrests directly, restricting their ability to independently document the operation. A coalition of Canadian news organizations went to court, and on July 20, 2021, Justice Douglas Thompson found the RCMP had not justified the extensive exclusion zones it had imposed on media access. The judge ordered that future enforcement decisions be made with an explicit reminder of the media's role in a free and democratic society and the need to avoid unnecessary interference with journalism. The RCMP had defended the restrictions as reasonably necessary given hazardous terrain, limited space for enforcement and poor cell coverage.{c:471}{c:472}{c:473}
stated_justification: The RCMP said the restrictions were "reasonably necessary" because of hazardous terrain, limited space to safely conduct enforcement, and poor cell phone coverage at the blockade sites.{c:472}
effect_on_reporting: Journalists had been kept at a distance from arrests and enforcement actions for weeks under an escort system that limited independent verification of how the operation was being conducted, before the court intervened.{c:471}{c:472}{c:473}

title: Australia's High Court invalidates warrant for raid on journalist Annika Smethurst
issue_of_the_day: The 2019 raid stemmed from Smethurst's reporting on leaked, classified plans to expand the Australian Signals Directorate's domestic surveillance powers, which the government treated as a national-security leak investigation.
outcome_note: The High Court found the 2019 warrant invalid, and the AFP announced weeks later it would not charge Smethurst.
summary: Australia's High Court ruled that the warrant the Australian Federal Police used to raid News Corp journalist Annika Smethurst's home over a national-security leak was invalid, and weeks later the AFP said it would not lay charges against her, citing insufficient evidence.{c:474}
what_happened: The Australian Federal Police had searched journalist Annika Smethurst's Canberra home in 2019 over her reporting on leaked documents describing plans to expand the Australian Signals Directorate's powers to monitor Australians domestically. Smethurst challenged the warrant, and on April 15, 2020, Australia's High Court unanimously ruled it invalid because it failed to properly specify the offense being investigated, though the court allowed police to keep the seized material for any future prosecution. On May 27, 2020, AFP Deputy Commissioner Ian McCartney announced the agency would not charge Smethurst, saying there was insufficient evidence to establish the path the leaked document had taken or who had provided it. The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance said the case showed how national-security laws could be misused against legitimate public-interest journalism, and the Law Council of Australia's president said the law still left journalists exposed to investigation and prosecution.{c:474}{c:475}{c:476}{c:477}
stated_justification: The AFP said its investigation could not establish, with sufficient evidence, how the leaked document had moved or who had provided it to Smethurst.{c:474}{c:475}{c:476}{c:477}
effect_on_reporting: A journalist's home was searched and her devices seized over a story about government surveillance powers, and although the warrant was ultimately found invalid and no charges followed, press-freedom groups said the case showed reporters remained exposed to similar national-security investigations.{c:476}

title: China expels American journalists from three major U.S. newspapers
issue_of_the_day: The expulsions followed a rapid exchange of measures: a Wall Street Journal opinion piece China objected to, the U.S. capping Chinese state-media staff, and China's decision to expel American reporters from three outlets in response, all unfolding as the coronavirus pandemic was spreading globally.
outcome_note: The expelled journalists' press credentials were not restored; reciprocal media restrictions between the two countries continued for years afterward.
summary: China ordered American correspondents for The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post to leave the country, in a reciprocal response to the Trump administration capping the number of Chinese state-media employees allowed in the United States, which itself followed China's earlier expulsion of three Journal reporters over an opinion headline.{c:478}
what_happened: In February 2020, after The Wall Street Journal published an opinion column China's government objected to, Beijing revoked the press credentials of three Journal reporters based in China. On March 2, 2020, the Trump administration capped the number of Chinese state-media employees allowed to work in the United States at 100, down from about 160. On March 17, 2020, China's foreign ministry announced it would require American journalists working for The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post whose press cards were due to expire that year to leave the country, and said they would not be allowed to work as journalists in mainland China, Hong Kong or Macau. China's foreign ministry called the move "entirely necessary and reciprocal countermeasures" against what it described as American measures aimed exclusively at Chinese media organizations. U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo said he regretted China's decision to further limit free press operations worldwide.{c:478}{c:479}{c:480}
stated_justification: China's foreign ministry described the expulsions as "entirely necessary and reciprocal countermeasures," saying "what the US has done is exclusively targeting Chinese media organizations, and hence driven by a Cold War mentality."{c:479}
effect_on_reporting: American correspondents for three of the country's largest newspapers lost their accreditation to report from mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau at the outset of the global coronavirus pandemic, cutting into independent Western reporting from China during a major global story.{c:478}{c:479}{c:480}
unknowns: The precise number of journalists affected across the three outlets was not specified in the source reviewed.

title: Zimbabwe's Patriotic Act criminalizes journalists' contact with foreign governments
issue_of_the_day: The bill passed weeks before Zimbabwe's August 2023 general election, at a time when the government accused foreign-linked civil-society and media figures of working to undermine it ahead of the vote.
outcome_note: President Mnangagwa signed the bill into law despite CPJ's call for a veto; a court challenge by journalists did not block it.
summary: President Emmerson Mnangagwa signed the Patriotic Act, which criminalizes meeting foreign governments or officials with intent to harm Zimbabwe's sovereignty, with penalties up to death for advocating armed intervention and up to ten years for supporting sanctions, weeks before the country's 2023 general election.{c:483}
what_happened: Zimbabwe's parliament passed the Criminal Law Amendment (Patriotic Act) in June 2023, and President Emmerson Mnangagwa signed it into law on July 14, 2023. The law criminalizes meetings with foreign governments or their agents intended to subvert, overthrow or damage Zimbabwe's sovereignty, with penalties as severe as life imprisonment or death for advocating armed intervention, and up to ten years in prison or a fine for advocating sanctions or trade boycotts against the country. The Committee to Protect Journalists' Angela Quintal said journalists must be free to report and meet whomever they choose, including foreign diplomats, without risking imprisonment, and called on Mnangagwa to reject the bill. Information Minister Monica Mutsvangwa said the law did not criminalize journalists' ordinary work but only meetings intended to injure the country's sovereignty. Zimbabwean journalist Dumisani Muleya asked whether an interview eliciting an unfavorable answer could itself be treated as a crime under the law.{c:481}{c:482}{c:483}{c:484}
stated_justification: Information Minister Monica Mutsvangwa said the bill "did not criminalize journalists' work in Zimbabwe but barred meetings with foreign governments...that have 'the intention to injure the sovereignty.'"{c:482}
effect_on_reporting: Zimbabwean journalists who interview foreign diplomats or officials, a routine part of covering international affairs, faced the risk that authorities could later characterize such contact as intended to damage the country's sovereignty, carrying penalties as severe as life imprisonment.{c:481}{c:484}
